conversation.content: This is an outpatient headache clinic consultation at a community teaching hospital in Houston, Texas. The clinician is Dr. Gabriela Ochoa-Salinas, a neurologist with headache medicine training. The patient is Adaeze Okonkwo, a 38-year-old woman (68 kg, 165 cm) referred by her primary care physician for frequent headaches. Laboratory results drawn by her primary care physician one week earlier are available. The encounter includes an initial visit and a six-week follow-up visit. Maintain a professional, clinically precise tone.

Good morning, Doctor. My primary care doctor sent me here because I have had a headache almost every day for months. I am honestly worried something is wrong in my head. I have never had headaches like this before this year.

Good morning, Ms. Okonkwo. I am Dr. Ochoa-Salinas. Thank you for coming in, and I want to make sure we take that worry seriously and answer it properly. Let us start with the pattern. When did these headaches begin, and how many days in a typical month do you have any headache at all, even a mild one? Where do you feel the pain, and how would you describe it: pressing or tightening, throbbing or pulsating, stabbing, or something else? On a 0 to 10 scale, how strong is a typical day and a bad day?

They started around the beginning of the year, so about five months ago. Now I would say I have a headache most days, maybe 18 or 19 days a month. It feels like a tight band around my forehead and the back of my head, both sides, like someone is squeezing. Usually it is a 4 or 5, sometimes a 6 in the late afternoon. It is not throbbing. I can still work through it and climbing the stairs at the office does not make it worse. Once in a while bright screens bother me a little, but I never throw up and I am not nauseous.

That description is very helpful: bilateral, band-like pressure, mild to moderate intensity, not worsened by routine activity, and no nausea. Before I draw any conclusions, I need to rule out features that would point toward a secondary cause. Please answer each of these carefully.

1. Has any headache come on suddenly and reached maximum intensity within about a minute, like a thunderclap?
2. Do headaches wake you from sleep, or are they clearly worse lying down, on coughing or straining, or on standing up?
3. Any weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, double vision, loss of vision, or transient visual blurring?
4. Any fever, weight loss, night sweats, or recent infection?
5. Any head injury in the past year?
6. When was your last menstrual period, and is there any chance of pregnancy?
7. Any new medications, including hormonal contraception?

No to all of those, I think. Nothing sudden, it builds up slowly during the day. It does not wake me up. No weakness or vision problems, no fever, no injury. My period finished about two weeks ago and I have had a copper IUD for three years, no hormones. My mother keeps telling me it is 'too much thinking' and to rub Robb on my temples. That is the mentholated balm everyone back home uses. It helps a little, honestly.

Those are reassuring answers, and your mother may be closer to the mark than you would expect. My own grandmother in Laredo reached for a jar of mentholated rub for every ache in the family, and topical menthol is harmless and can give modest relief for this kind of pain, so there is no reason to stop using it. Stress and sustained concentration are well-recognized triggers for the type of headache you are describing.

Now I need an accurate picture of your medications, because this matters a great deal for frequent headaches. What do you take when you have a headache, what dose, and on how many days per month? Please include anything over the counter, anything borrowed, and any leftover prescriptions.

Just Tylenol, the extra-strength kind. Maybe two times a week, not a big deal. I do not like taking pills. I do have some tramadol left over from when I hurt my back last year, but I have not used it for this. Oh, and a coworker gets the same headaches and her doctor gave her Flexeril. She said it works well. Could I try that? I also brought my phone, I have been logging the headaches in an app like my doctor asked.

Thank you for keeping a diary; that is exactly what helps us most. Would you mind if we look at it together? I would rather base the plan on your actual log than on anyone's memory, including mine, because the details of the busiest months tend to blur.

I see the app records both headache days and a medication column. Over the last 30 days it shows headache on **19 days**, and a pill entry on **21 days**, several of them marked 'Tylenol x2' in the morning and 'Aleve' in the afternoon. That is quite different from two times a week. I am not raising this to criticize you. Almost everyone with daily headaches during a heavy work period ends up taking more than they realize, and it is one of the most important things for me to understand. Can you walk me through what a usual day looks like?

Okay. You are right, and I am a bit embarrassed. I did not want you to think I was abusing pills. During tax season I have been taking two extra-strength Tylenol most mornings before the pain gets bad, so it does not ruin my day, and then two Aleve in the afternoon maybe two or three times a week. On really bad days I take two more Tylenol at night. This has been going on since about February, so about four months.

I appreciate you telling me that plainly; it changes the plan in a useful way, not a bad one. Two extra-strength tablets are **1000 mg of acetaminophen**, and two Aleve are **440 mg of naproxen sodium**. Taking a simple analgesic on 15 or more days a month for more than three months can itself sustain daily headache, a condition called medication-overuse headache. You have been at about 21 days a month for roughly four months, so you meet that threshold. Your total acetaminophen on the bad days, 2000 mg, stays within safe liver limits, which is good.

Let me examine you now. I will check your blood pressure, look at the back of your eyes, do a full neurological examination, and press on the muscles of your scalp, jaw, and neck.
Okay. Some of those spots on my neck and the back of my head were really sore when you pressed. What did you find?

Here are your findings.

**Vital signs:** BP **124/78 mmHg** (repeat 122/76 mmHg), HR **72 bpm**, RR **14/min**, temperature **36.8 C**, SpO2 **99%** on room air. Weight **68 kg**, height 165 cm, BMI **25.0 kg/m2** (68 / 1.65 squared = 24.98).

**Fundoscopy:** sharp optic disc margins with spontaneous venous pulsations in both eyes, so there is no papilledema. Corrected visual acuity 20/20 in each eye, full visual fields to confrontation.

**Neurological examination:** pupils equal and reactive, extraocular movements full, facial sensation and strength symmetric. Strength 5/5 throughout, no pronator drift, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, plantar responses flexor. Finger-nose and tandem gait normal, Romberg negative. No neck stiffness or meningismus.

**Pericranial tenderness:** using the standardized Total Tenderness Score, which grades eight paired muscle and tendon sites from 0 to 3 for a maximum of 48, you scored **19/48**, most marked over the trapezius, suboccipital, and temporalis muscles. Jaw opening is 44 mm with no joint clicking. Neck range of motion is full with discomfort at end range.

In short: a completely normal neurological examination with increased tenderness of the head and neck muscles, which is characteristic of the headache type I suspect.
That is a relief about my eyes and nerves. But should I get an MRI to be sure? And my doctor did blood work last week, did that show anything?

Your primary care physician's labs from last week are all within normal limits:

- Hemoglobin **12.6 g/dL** (12.0-15.5), MCV 86 fL (80-100), WBC 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 256 x10^9/L (150-400)
- Sodium **139 mmol/L** (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.1), chloride **104 mmol/L** (98-107), bicarbonate **25 mmol/L** (22-29); anion gap 139 - (104 + 25) = **10 mmol/L** (8-16)
- BUN 12 mg/dL (7-20), creatinine **0.8 mg/dL** (0.5-1.1), glucose 88 mg/dL (70-99), calcium 9.4 mg/dL (8.6-10.2)
- ALT **18 U/L** (7-35), AST 21 U/L (10-35)
- TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), ferritin 42 ng/mL (15-150)

Your estimated creatinine clearance by Cockcroft-Gault is (140 - 38) x 68 / (72 x 0.8) x 0.85 = **about 102 mL/min**, and normal liver enzymes mean both acetaminophen and anti-inflammatory medicines remain options when used within limits.

Regarding the MRI: with a stable pattern over five months, no red-flag features, and a normal neurological and fundoscopic examination, imaging is very unlikely to find a cause and is not recommended. Scans in this setting commonly turn up incidental findings that create anxiety without changing treatment. If any red flag appears later, I would order one without hesitation.
So what is actually causing this? Please give it to me straight.

You have two overlapping diagnoses.

**1. Chronic tension-type headache with pericranial tenderness.** By the international criteria (ICHD-3), this means headache on 15 or more days a month for more than three months, lasting hours or continuous, with at least two of these four features: bilateral location, pressing or tightening quality, mild or moderate intensity, and no aggravation by routine physical activity. You have all four. In the chronic form, one of photophobia, phonophobia, or mild nausea is still allowed, so your occasional sensitivity to bright screens fits, provided there is no moderate or severe nausea or vomiting.

**2. Medication-overuse headache, mainly from acetaminophen.** The near-daily analgesic use is likely keeping the pain system in a sensitized state so that headaches recur each day.

The mechanism of the chronic form is thought to involve increased sensitivity of pain pathways in the brain and spinal cord, driven by prolonged input from tender head and neck muscles. That is why treatment works on two fronts: reducing the analgesic exposure and calming that sensitized system.
So I have to stop the Tylenol and Aleve? How am I supposed to get through a workday? What can I take when it is bad?

The plan is to stop the daily pattern, not to leave you without any relief.

**Withdrawal:** stop the routine morning acetaminophen and the afternoon naproxen now. Simple analgesics can be stopped abruptly and safely. Expect the headaches to feel worse for roughly one to two weeks before improving; that worsening is a sign of withdrawal, not of anything dangerous.

**Acute treatment, limited to no more than 2 days per week (under 10 days per month):**
- **Naproxen (Naprosyn) 500 mg** with food, about **7.4 mg/kg** at your weight; a second 500 mg dose may be taken after 12 hours if needed, maximum **1000 mg in 24 hours**.
- Or **acetaminophen (Tylenol) 1000 mg**, about **14.7 mg/kg**, maximum **3000 mg in 24 hours**.
- If naproxen proves ineffective, **diclofenac (Voltaren) 50 mg** orally, about **0.74 mg/kg**, is an alternative NSAID. Never take two NSAIDs on the same day, and do not add over-the-counter Aleve or ibuprofen on top.

The Naprosyn 500 mg tablet and oral diclofenac are prescription products; I will send both. The European Federation of Neurological Societies guideline supports simple analgesics and NSAIDs for acute treatment and stresses that frequent use must be avoided to prevent medication-overuse headache (PMID: 20482606). Please record every dose in your app.

I understand. But if I only treat two days a week, what about the other days? Is there something that prevents them? My doctor mentioned amitriptyline but I read that it is an antidepressant. I am not depressed.

That concern comes up often, and it is reasonable. Amitriptyline is used here at low doses for its effect on pain pathways, not for mood. The starting doses we use for headache prevention are well below those used for depression. The EFNS guideline names amitriptyline the drug of first choice for preventing chronic tension-type headache (PMID: 20482606). In a placebo-controlled crossover trial in non-depressed patients with chronic tension-type headache, amitriptyline reduced the area under the headache curve by 30% compared with placebo, while citalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, had no significant effect; that difference suggests its benefit comes from mechanisms beyond serotonin alone (PMID: 8795600).

**Dosing plan (Elavil / amitriptyline):**
- Start **10 mg** once nightly (about **0.15 mg/kg**), taken 1 to 2 hours before bedtime.
- Increase by 10 mg every 2 weeks as tolerated: 20 mg, then **30 mg** (about 0.44 mg/kg). Many patients do well at 20 to 30 mg; the usual maintenance range is 30 to 75 mg.
- It takes 4 to 8 weeks to judge benefit. Our target is at least a 50% reduction in headache days.

**Expected side effects:** dry mouth, morning drowsiness, constipation, some appetite increase, and lightheadedness on standing. Avoid driving if you feel groggy, and limit alcohol, which adds sedation. I obtained a baseline ECG today because tricyclics can affect cardiac conduction: sinus rhythm at 70 bpm, PR 152 ms, QTc **412 ms**, all normal.
Okay, I can try that. What about the tramadol I have at home, or the Flexeril my coworker takes? If the amitriptyline is not enough, could I use those on the bad days?

No to both, and the reasons are specific.

**Tramadol with amitriptyline is a major interaction.** Both increase serotonin activity, so together they raise the risk of serotonin syndrome: agitation, tremor, sweating, muscle twitching, fever, and a racing heart. Tramadol also lowers the seizure threshold, and amitriptyline does as well, so the combination compounds that risk. Separately, tramadol is an opioid, and opioids cause medication-overuse headache at lower frequencies than simple analgesics. Please return the leftover tablets to a pharmacy take-back program.

**MAO inhibitors are an absolute no with amitriptyline.** Combining a tricyclic with an MAO inhibitor can cause severe serotonin syndrome or a hypertensive crisis. This includes phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, rasagiline, the antibiotic linezolid, and methylene blue. A washout of at least 14 days is needed between an MAO inhibitor and amitriptyline. If any clinician, emergency department, or dentist proposes a new medicine, tell them you take amitriptyline.

**Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)** is structurally almost identical to a tricyclic antidepressant. Taken with amitriptyline, it stacks sedation, dry mouth, constipation, and serotonergic and cardiac effects, and it shares the same MAO inhibitor contraindication. The EFNS guideline also concludes that muscle relaxants should not be used for tension-type headache (PMID: 20482606). Your coworker's experience is real to her, but it is not a safe or evidence-based choice for you.

That makes sense. What else can I do besides medication? My job is stressful, I sit at a computer for eleven hours a day in tax season, and I drink a lot of coffee. On weekends the headache is sometimes worse.

Non-drug treatment is a core part of the plan, not an afterthought. In a randomized trial of 203 adults with chronic tension-type headache, tricyclic antidepressant medication and a brief stress-management program were each better than placebo. The combination was more likely to produce a 50% or greater reduction in headache activity, 64% of participants versus 38% with medication alone and 35% with stress management alone (PMID: 11325322). Medication worked faster; the skills helped sustain improvement.

**Specific steps:**
1. **Cognitive-behavioral stress management or EMG biofeedback.** I will refer you to our headache psychologist; EMG biofeedback has documented benefit in tension-type headache.
2. **Physical therapy** focused on cervical posture, trapezius and suboccipital release, and a home stretching routine.
3. **Workstation:** monitor at eye level, feet flat, and a 5-minute break every 50 minutes to roll the shoulders and stretch the neck.
4. **Caffeine:** tell me how much you drink.
5. **Sleep:** a consistent 7 to 8 hour window, including during deadlines.

Your weekend pattern suggests caffeine withdrawal, especially if you sleep later and drink less coffee on Saturdays.

Two large coffees on workdays, probably more than 300 milligrams, and almost nothing on weekends. I never connected that. I will cut back slowly. I will see you in six weeks.

[Six weeks later] Hello again, Doctor. I did what you said. The first ten days off the daily pills were hard, but it got better. I have been on 20 mg of amitriptyline for four weeks. My mouth is dry and I am groggy in the mornings until about 9 a.m. Here is my app.

Welcome back. The first two weeks after stopping daily analgesics are the hardest part, and you came through them. Here are the comparisons from your diary over the last 30 days against the first visit:

- Headache days: **11**, down from 19, a **42%** reduction
- Days with any acute medication: **6**, down from 21
- Days with pain of 5 or higher: **3**
- Caffeine reduced to one medium coffee daily, same on weekends

**Today's vitals:** BP **118/76 mmHg** seated, **114/74 mmHg** standing, HR 78 bpm seated and 86 bpm standing, so no orthostatic hypotension. Weight **68.9 kg**, a 0.9 kg gain.

You are improving but have not yet reached the 50% target, and the morning grogginess tells me you are taking the dose too late. What time do you take it?

Usually around 10:30 at night, right before I fall asleep. I sometimes forget and take it at midnight. How long will I have to be on this medicine? And my husband and I are talking about maybe having a baby in the next year or two. Does that change anything?

Moving the dose earlier should fix most of the grogginess. Take it at **8:00 p.m.**, 2 to 3 hours before sleep. Once the mornings are clear for 2 weeks, increase to **30 mg** nightly and keep the diary going. For dry mouth, sugar-free lozenges and frequent water help. If constipation develops, increase fiber and fluids.

**Duration:** once you reach good control, we continue for about **6 to 12 months**, then taper by 10 mg every 1 to 2 weeks rather than stopping abruptly.

**Pregnancy planning:** this does change the plan, and I am glad you raised it early. Please tell me before you remove the IUD, so we can taper amitriptyline beforehand and rely more on the behavioral and physical therapy strategies. In pregnancy, acetaminophen at the lowest effective dose is the preferred acute option. NSAIDs, including naproxen and diclofenac, should be avoided from 20 weeks of gestation onward because of risks to fetal kidney function and the ductus arteriosus, and they are generally best avoided while trying to conceive. We will make a written pre-conception plan together.
Thank you. Can you summarize what I need to do, and tell me what would mean I should call you or go to the emergency room?

Your plan:

1. **Amitriptyline:** 20 mg at 8:00 p.m. nightly; increase to 30 mg after 2 weeks of clear mornings.
2. **Acute treatment, no more than 2 days per week:** naproxen 500 mg with food (maximum 1000 mg/24 h) **or** acetaminophen 1000 mg (maximum 3000 mg/24 h); diclofenac 50 mg as the NSAID alternative, never two NSAIDs on the same day.
3. **Do not take:** tramadol, cyclobenzaprine, or any MAO inhibitor with amitriptyline. Mention amitriptyline to every prescriber and pharmacist.
4. **Non-drug care:** headache psychology (stress management and biofeedback), physical therapy, workstation breaks, steady caffeine, regular sleep.
5. **Diary:** log every headache day and every dose.

**Go to the emergency department immediately for:** a sudden severe headache peaking within a minute; headache with fever and neck stiffness; new weakness, numbness, confusion, speech or vision loss; a seizure; or headache after a head injury.

**Call the clinic for:** a change in the pattern of your headaches, headaches that become worse lying down or on coughing, palpitations or fainting, severe constipation or difficulty urinating, or low mood.

I will see you in 8 weeks. You are on a good path, and the diary will show us the next steps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Accepting the patient's estimate of analgesic use without checking a diary or pharmacy history
common_mistakes.explanation: Patients with near-daily headache routinely underestimate their analgesic intake. Simple analgesic use on 15 or more days per month for more than 3 months establishes medication-overuse headache, which perpetuates chronic tension-type headache and blunts the response to amitriptyline unless the overuse is withdrawn.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ordering MRI or CT for a stable, bilateral, pressing headache with a normal neurological and fundoscopic examination
common_mistakes.explanation: Neuroimaging has very low diagnostic yield when there are no red flags (thunderclap onset, positional or Valsalva worsening, papilledema, focal deficits, systemic features, age over 50 at onset). Incidental findings increase anxiety and cost without changing management; imaging should be reserved for red-flag presentations.

common_mistakes.mistake: Prescribing muscle relaxants such as cyclobenzaprine, or opioids such as tramadol, for tension-type headache
common_mistakes.explanation: The EFNS guideline states that muscle relaxants and opioids should not be used for tension-type headache. Cyclobenzaprine is structurally a tricyclic and adds sedation, anticholinergic, and serotonergic burden to amitriptyline; tramadol with amitriptyline raises serotonin syndrome and seizure risk, and opioids cause medication-overuse headache at lower thresholds.

common_mistakes.mistake: Starting amitriptyline at a high dose or judging it ineffective after 1 to 2 weeks
common_mistakes.explanation: Amitriptyline should be started at 10 mg nightly and titrated by 10 to 25 mg every 1 to 2 weeks to a maintenance of roughly 30 to 75 mg, taken 1 to 2 hours before bedtime. Benefit takes 4 to 8 weeks to judge; rapid escalation causes sedation and anticholinergic effects that drive premature discontinuation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Misclassifying chronic tension-type headache as migraine because of one mild associated feature
common_mistakes.explanation: ICHD-3 chronic tension-type headache allows no more than one of photophobia, phonophobia, or mild nausea, but no moderate or severe nausea and no vomiting. A single mild feature alongside bilateral, pressing, non-aggravated pain does not make the diagnosis migraine, and treating it with triptans is not indicated.

differential_diagnosis.differentiating_factors: Migraine features on at least 8 headache days per month: often unilateral, pulsating, moderate to severe, aggravated by routine activity, with nausea or with both photophobia and phonophobia. Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate, not worsened by activity, and has at most one mild associated feature in the chronic form.

Headache on 15 or more days per month in a patient with a pre-existing headache disorder and regular overuse for more than 3 months (simple analgesics on 15 or more days per month; triptans, opioids, or combination analgesics on 10 or more days per month). Often coexists with chronic tension-type headache and improves after withdrawal.

Daily headache typically in women of childbearing age with elevated BMI, often worse lying down or with Valsalva, accompanied by transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, and papilledema on fundoscopy. Normal optic discs with spontaneous venous pulsations argue strongly against it.

Daily and unremitting headache from a distinct, clearly remembered onset, becoming continuous within 24 hours. Chronic tension-type headache instead evolves gradually from episodic headache, as in this patient's slow increase in frequency over months.

Usually unilateral, side-locked pain originating in the neck, provoked by neck movement or sustained posture, with reduced cervical range of motion and pain reproduced by pressure over upper cervical structures. Tension-type headache is bilateral with full neck range of motion and diffuse pericranial tenderness.

related_diseases.relationship: Frequent analgesic use to treat tension-type headache can transform or sustain chronic daily headache; withdrawal of the overused medication is a prerequisite for effective prevention.

Frequently coexists with tension-type headache in the same patient; distinguishing the two headache types in the diary guides acute treatment choice, since triptans are ineffective for tension-type headache.

Psychiatric comorbidity is common in chronic tension-type headache, lowers pain thresholds, and influences response to treatment; screening and cognitive-behavioral therapy are part of comprehensive care.
Shares pericranial muscle tenderness (temporalis, masseter) and central sensitization mechanisms; bruxism and jaw dysfunction can aggravate tension-type headache.

related_diseases.disease: Myofascial pain syndrome of the neck and shoulders
related_diseases.relationship: Trapezius and suboccipital trigger points contribute peripheral nociceptive input that is thought to drive central sensitization in chronic tension-type headache; physical therapy targets this component.

original.executive_summary: **Chronic tension-type headache with pericranial tenderness (ICHD-3 2.3.1) complicated by medication-overuse headache** in a 38-year-old woman (68 kg) with 19 headache days per month and undisclosed analgesic use on 21 days per month, identified tactfully through her headache diary. Examination, fundoscopy, and laboratory tests were normal (anion gap 10 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, CrCl about 102 mL/min, ALT 18 U/L); Total Tenderness Score 19/48; no imaging indicated. Management: abrupt withdrawal of daily acetaminophen and naproxen; acute naproxen 500 mg, acetaminophen 1000 mg, or diclofenac 50 mg limited to 2 days per week; amitriptyline 10 mg nightly titrated to 30 mg with baseline QTc 412 ms (EFNS first-line, PMID: 20482606; PMID: 8795600); stress management, biofeedback, and physical therapy (combined therapy superior, PMID: 11325322). Counseled against tramadol (serotonin syndrome, seizure threshold), MAO inhibitors (serotonin syndrome, hypertensive crisis), and cyclobenzaprine. At 6 weeks: headache days 19 to 11 (42% reduction), acute medication days 21 to 6; dose timing moved earlier and titration continued, with pre-conception planning for amitriptyline taper and avoidance of NSAIDs from 20 weeks of gestation.

original.name: Epilepsy
original.description: Epilepsy is defined as a brain disorder characterized by an enduring predisposition to generate epileptic seizures, defined practically as two unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, or one unprovoked seizure with >60% recurrence risk. It affects 1-3% of the world population and has diverse etiologies (structural, genetic, metabolic, immune, infectious, unknown). Seizure classification (focal vs. generalized; motor vs. non-motor) guides treatment choice. Most patients achieve seizure freedom with one or two antiepileptic drugs.

drug_interactions.description: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4/CYP2C9 metabolism of valproic acid, reducing valproic acid levels; valproic acid inhibits carbamazepine's epoxide hydrolase, increasing toxic carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide levels causing nausea, diplopia, ataxia.
Phenytoin induces CYP2C19 and glucuronidation of lamotrigine, reducing lamotrigine levels by 40-50%; dose adjustment of lamotrigine required when adding or removing phenytoin.

original.patient_scenario: Marisol Reyes Castaneda is a 27-year-old Mexican-American woman who works as a bookkeeper at a credit union. She is seen 16 days after an emergency department visit for a witnessed generalized convulsion at work; on history she has had a year of unrecognized spells of rising epigastric sensation and deja vu, some followed by staring and automatisms, and she had a prolonged febrile seizure at 18 months of age. She was discharged from the ED on levetiracetam, takes a combined oral contraceptive, and hopes to have children in a few years.

conversation.content: This is a new-patient visit in an academic comprehensive epilepsy center. The assistant is Dr. Katerina Vlahos, an epileptologist. The user is Marisol Reyes Castaneda, a 27-year-old right-handed woman referred after an emergency department visit 16 days ago for a witnessed convulsive seizure. Available records: ED note with vitals, blood gas and chemistry; routine EEG (day 9); 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI brain (day 12); pre-visit laboratory panel drawn two days ago including a levetiracetam trough. The clinician should take a precise semiological history, interpret data accurately, classify seizures using ILAE 2017 terminology, choose therapy appropriate to a woman of childbearing potential, and counsel on interactions, safety and follow-up in a measured, professional register.

Hi, Dr. Vlahos. I'm Marisol. So about two weeks ago I had a seizure at work, at least that's what everyone says, because I don't remember any of it. I was at my desk and then I woke up on the floor with paramedics around me and my tongue was bleeding. The ER doctor said it was probably a one-time thing from stress and gave me Keppra. I've never had anything like that before in my life, so I'm honestly hoping this is just a follow-up to say I'm fine.

I'm glad you came in, Marisol, and I understand wanting this to be a single event. Before I can tell you that, I need to understand what happened in more detail, because the answer depends heavily on history, not only on the tests.

Let me start with the minutes and months before the convulsion. Some people have brief spells for a long time that they never think of as seizures. Over the past year or so, have you had any episodes where you suddenly felt a strange rising sensation in your stomach, an intense feeling that you had lived this exact moment before, an unusual smell or taste, or a sense of fear that came out of nowhere? And has anyone ever told you that you stared, did not answer them, or made chewing or lip-smacking movements for a minute or so?

Oh. Actually, yes, now that you say it like that. For maybe a year I've had these weird moments where my stomach feels like it's floating up into my chest and I get the strongest deja vu, like I already know what the next person is going to say. Sometimes there's a smell like burnt rubber. It lasts less than a minute. I thought it was anxiety. And my coworker Denise told me a few months ago that I stared at her and kept rubbing papers on my desk and didn't answer her. I didn't remember that part, I just felt tired and couldn't find my words for a few minutes after.

That is very important information, and thank you for describing it so clearly. What you are describing are almost certainly seizures that begin in one part of the brain, which we call focal seizures.

- The rising stomach sensation, deja vu and burnt smell, when you stay fully aware, are **focal aware seizures**; people often call them auras.
- The spells where you stared, fumbled with papers and did not respond, and do not remember afterwards, are **focal impaired awareness seizures**.
- The event at work, where a focal seizure spread to both sides of the brain and caused stiffening and jerking, is a **focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure**.

These are the categories in the International League Against Epilepsy operational classification (PMID: 28276060), and the distinction matters because it points to where the seizures start and which medicines work best.

A few more details help me localize further. Which hand did Denise see you fumble with, and did she notice the other arm doing anything? Are you right- or left-handed? Did anyone describe your head or eyes turning to one side before the convulsion at work? Did you ever have a seizure with fever as a small child? And in the days before the big event, how was your sleep, and were you drinking alcohol?

I'm right-handed. Denise said my left hand was rubbing the papers and my right arm was kind of stiff and bent up against my chest. At the big one, my manager said my head turned to the right and then I went stiff and started shaking, maybe two minutes. My mom says I had a really long seizure with a high fever when I was about a year and a half, like more than twenty minutes, and they kept me in the hospital. Sleep was terrible that week. It was quarter-end closing and I was sleeping maybe four hours a night for three nights. I barely drink, maybe a glass of wine at a birthday.

Those details fit together in a very consistent way.

- **Left-hand automatisms with right-arm dystonic posturing**: automatisms tend to occur in the hand on the same side as the seizure onset, and the stiff, posturing arm is usually on the opposite side. That pattern points to the **left temporal lobe**.
- **Word-finding difficulty afterwards** in a right-handed person suggests the seizure involved the language-dominant left hemisphere.
- **Head turning to the right** just before the convulsion is forced turning away from the side of onset, again consistent with the left.
- **A prolonged febrile seizure in infancy** is a well-known risk factor for scarring in the hippocampus, a structure deep in the temporal lobe.

The sleep deprivation almost certainly lowered your threshold that week, but it is a trigger, not a cause.

Now the ED record. On arrival your vitals were **BP 152/94 mmHg, HR 122 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 93% on room air** (98% on 2 L nasal cannula), **temperature 37.7 C**, fingerstick glucose **131 mg/dL**. That pattern of high heart rate, blood pressure and mild temperature rise is typical right after a convulsion.

The arterial blood gas at 15 minutes showed **pH 7.25** (7.35-7.45), **PaCO2 44 mmHg** (35-45), **HCO3 18.5 mEq/L** (22-26). Those three values are internally consistent: 6.1 + log(18.5 / (0.03 x 44)) = 7.25. Chemistry: **Na 139** (135-145), **K 3.8** (3.5-5.1), **Cl 101** (98-107), **CO2 19 mEq/L** (22-29), giving an **anion gap of 139 - (101 + 19) = 19** (reference 8-16), with **lactate 5.9 mmol/L** (0.5-2.2). For a bicarbonate of 18.5 the expected PaCO2 would be about 34-38 mmHg, so a PaCO2 of 44 means there was also some post-ictal under-breathing: a mixed lactic metabolic and respiratory acidosis. The key point is that two hours later your **CO2 was 24, Cl 103, anion gap 12, lactate 1.3 mmol/L**. Lactate from muscle activity that clears that quickly is exactly what we expect after a generalized convulsion.

Okay, so that was just from the shaking. Did they find anything else in the blood that caused it, like low sugar or low sodium? Because if it was something like that, then it's not really epilepsy, right?

That is the right question, and they checked for those causes carefully. Glucose was **131 mg/dL**, sodium **139 mEq/L**, calcium **9.3 mg/dL** (8.6-10.3), magnesium **2.0 mg/dL** (1.7-2.2), creatinine **0.72 mg/dL** (0.5-1.1). Blood alcohol was not detected, the urine drug screen was negative, and the urine pregnancy test was negative. The white count of **12.6 x10^3/uL** (4.0-11.0) is a stress effect of the convulsion, not infection. A prolactin drawn 20 minutes after the event was **52 ng/mL** (4.8-23.3), and CK at 6 hours was **410 U/L** (26-192); both support a true generalized convulsion.

So nothing acutely provoked this seizure. Under the ILAE practical definition, epilepsy is diagnosed after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or after one unprovoked seizure when the risk of another is at least 60% (PMID: 24730690). You have had many unprovoked focal seizures over roughly a year plus one focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure, so you meet the definition on the first criterion alone. I know that is different from what you heard in the ED, and it is not what you were hoping for. The ED team only had the convulsion to go on; the earlier spells change the picture.
That's a lot to take in. What did the brain wave test and the MRI show? Nobody has called me with those results.

I'm sorry nobody went over them with you. Here they are.

**EEG (day 9, 60 minutes, including drowsiness and light sleep):** the background rhythm was normal at 10 Hz. There were **frequent sharp waves over the left anterior temporal region**, maximal at the F7 and T7 electrodes, increasing in sleep, and **intermittent rhythmic slowing over the left temporal region**. No seizures were recorded. These findings indicate a region of the left temporal lobe that is prone to generating seizures.

**MRI brain (3 Tesla, epilepsy protocol, day 12):** the **left hippocampus is smaller than the right, with increased T2/FLAIR signal and loss of its normal internal structure**, consistent with **left mesial temporal sclerosis**. There is no tumor, bleed, stroke or malformation elsewhere.

The history, the EEG and the MRI all point to the same place. The most likely explanation is that the long febrile seizure you had as an infant injured the left hippocampus, and years later that scarred tissue began producing seizures. The diagnosis is **focal epilepsy of structural etiology, left mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis**. That is actually a clear, well-understood form of epilepsy, and there are good treatment options at every stage.
Okay. At least there's a reason. The Keppra has been fine. I take it every morning and every night, I haven't missed a single dose since the ER.

Let me share today's exam and the labs from two days ago, and then we can talk about the medication.

**Vitals today:** BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 74 bpm, RR 14/min, temperature 36.7 C, SpO2 99% on room air, **weight 64.0 kg, height 162 cm, BMI 24.4 kg/m2**. Your neurological exam is normal: language, memory testing, cranial nerves, strength, coordination and gait are all intact. There is a healing laceration on the **left lateral border of the tongue**, which fits a convulsive seizure.

**Pre-visit labs:** Na 140, K 4.1, Cl 104, CO2 25 mEq/L, anion gap 11, BUN 11 mg/dL, creatinine 0.68 mg/dL, AST 19 U/L, ALT 16 U/L, CBC normal, pregnancy test negative.

The one result I want to ask you about is the levetiracetam level. On 500 mg twice daily we would expect a measurable level, and the usual reference range is **12-46 mcg/mL**. Yours came back **below the limit of detection, under 2.0 mcg/mL**. Levetiracetam has a half-life of about 6 to 8 hours, so a level that low usually means no dose has been taken for at least a couple of days. I'm not asking in order to judge you. Many people stop this particular medicine, often for very understandable reasons, and I would much rather know so the plan fits what is really happening. Has it been hard to take it?

Okay, yeah. I'm sorry. I stopped it about a week ago. I felt awful on it. I was snapping at my husband over nothing, crying in the car on the way to work, and I just felt like a different person. I didn't want to say it because I thought you'd think I wasn't taking this seriously.

Thank you for telling me. What you describe is a recognized side effect of levetiracetam: irritability, low mood and emotional lability affect roughly one in ten adults who take it, and it usually resolves once the drug is lowered or stopped. You were not being unserious; you were reacting to a real side effect. The timeline also fits, since you stopped around day 9 and the level was drawn on day 14, by which point the drug would have been fully cleared.

I do need to ask some direct questions because this matters for safety. Your intake questionnaire gave a **PHQ-9 score of 11**, in the moderate range. In the last two weeks, have you had any thoughts that you would be better off dead, or of hurting yourself in any way? Have you made any plans? Is anyone at home you would tell if you started feeling that way?

No, nothing like that. I never wanted to hurt myself. I just didn't feel like me. It's already better since I stopped. My husband noticed too. Honestly, can I just stay off everything? The seizure only happened because I didn't sleep.

I'm reassured by that answer, and I'm glad your husband is paying attention. Please keep one thing in mind regardless of which medicine you take: if dark thoughts ever appear, call us the same day, or call or text 988 at any hour.

On staying off medication, I would advise strongly against it, and here is why. Sleep loss lowered your threshold that week, but the auras and the staring spells were happening for a year during ordinary weeks. With **mesial temporal sclerosis, an abnormal EEG and ongoing focal seizures**, the chance of more seizures without treatment is very high, well above the 60% threshold we use to define epilepsy. Each further focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure carries risk of injury, and uncontrolled convulsive seizures are the main risk factor for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, which occurs in roughly 1 per 1,000 adults with epilepsy per year and more often when convulsions are not controlled. The goal of treatment is to stop both the big seizures and the auras.

The better question is which medicine. For newly diagnosed focal epilepsy the strongest head-to-head evidence comes from the SANAD II trial, which randomized adults to lamotrigine, levetiracetam or zonisamide. **Levetiracetam did not meet non-inferiority against lamotrigine** for time to 12-month remission, and lamotrigine was the most cost-effective option (PMID: 33838757). Lamotrigine also tends to be neutral or favorable for mood, which matters given what you just went through, and it has one of the best safety records in pregnancy. My recommendation is **lamotrigine**.
My cousin takes Depakote for her seizures and says it works really well. And my tia used to take Tegretol. Why not one of those?

Both are effective antiseizure medicines, and your relatives' experiences are real, but neither is the right first choice for you.

**Valproic acid (Depakote, Epival):** very effective for generalized epilepsies, but in anyone who could become pregnant it is the antiseizure medicine we avoid most. Exposure during pregnancy carries a major malformation risk of roughly 10%, including spina bifida, and is associated with lower IQ and higher rates of autism in children exposed in the womb. Regulators in several countries restrict its use in women of childbearing potential to situations where nothing else works. It can also cause weight gain, tremor, hair thinning and, rarely, liver injury or pancreatitis.

**Carbamazepine (Tegretol):** a good drug for focal epilepsy, but it is a strong enzyme inducer. It speeds the breakdown of oral contraceptive hormones enough to cause contraceptive failure, lowers vitamin D over time, and has a higher malformation risk than lamotrigine. It is also linked to serious skin reactions in people who carry certain HLA genes, so we genetically screen some patients before starting it.

There is also a specific interaction I want you to know about, because you may encounter these drugs elsewhere. If **carbamazepine and valproic acid** are ever combined, carbamazepine lowers valproate levels through enzyme induction, while valproate blocks the enzyme that clears **carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide**. The epoxide builds up and causes **nausea, double vision and unsteadiness**, often while the routine carbamazepine level looks normal, because that test does not measure the epoxide.

The same idea applies to **phenytoin (Dilantin)**, which ED teams sometimes load intravenously for prolonged seizures. Phenytoin induces the glucuronidation that clears lamotrigine and lowers **lamotrigine levels by roughly 40-50%**. If phenytoin were ever added, your lamotrigine dose would need to be increased, and if it were stopped, reduced. Please make sure any hospital knows you take lamotrigine.
That makes sense. I should tell you I'm on the birth control pill, Sprintec. And my husband and I want kids in maybe two years. Is lamotrigine okay with all of that?

I'm glad you raised both, because they change how I dose lamotrigine.

**The pill:** Sprintec contains ethinyl estradiol, and estrogen speeds up lamotrigine clearance. Lamotrigine levels can fall by about half while you are taking the active pills and then rise during the placebo week, which can cause dizziness or double vision that week or breakthrough seizures during active weeks. Lamotrigine does not reduce estrogen, though it may slightly lower the progestin level. There are two reasonable options:

1. **Switch to a levonorgestrel IUD.** It is highly effective, does not meaningfully interact with lamotrigine, and keeps your levels steady. This is my preferred option, and I can refer you to our women's health colleagues.
2. **Stay on the pill but take the active pills continuously** without the placebo week, and accept that you will likely need a higher lamotrigine dose, guided by blood levels.

If you ever stop an estrogen-containing pill while on lamotrigine, call us first, because your level could roughly double.

**Pregnancy:** lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the lowest major malformation rates among antiseizure medicines in the large pregnancy registries, about 2-3%, close to the background rate for any pregnancy. Please take **folic acid 1 mg daily** starting now, since about half of pregnancies are unplanned. When you are ready to try, we will meet beforehand: lamotrigine clearance rises sharply during pregnancy, so we check levels each trimester and adjust. Having a stable baseline level before pregnancy makes that much safer.
Okay. How do I start it? I read online that lamotrigine can cause a really bad rash.

You read correctly, and the slow start is designed around that risk. Serious rash, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, occurs in roughly 1 in 1,000 adults and is most likely in the first 8 weeks, with rapid titration, or when lamotrigine is combined with valproate. Starting low and going slow reduces that risk considerably.

At **64 kg**, and with no enzyme-inducing drugs or valproate on board, the schedule is:

- **Weeks 1-2:** 25 mg once daily (about 0.4 mg/kg/day)
- **Weeks 3-4:** 50 mg once daily
- **Week 5:** 50 mg twice daily
- **Week 6:** 75 mg twice daily
- **Week 7 onward:** **100 mg twice daily, 200 mg/day, about 3.1 mg/kg/day**

Two weeks after you reach 200 mg/day we check a trough lamotrigine level, drawn before the morning dose; the usual reference range is **2.5-15 mcg/mL**. If you remain on the combined pill, I expect to go higher, probably toward 300 mg/day.

If you develop **any rash, especially with fever, mouth or eye sores, blistering or skin pain**, stop lamotrigine and call us the same day or go to the ED. Do not restart on your own after a missed stretch of five or more half-lives, roughly 5 days, without calling, because restarting at full dose raises rash risk. One practical point: lamotrigine has been confused at pharmacies with drugs that have similar names, such as Lamisil, so check the tablet imprint each refill.

The hard part is the gap. Lamotrigine takes about 7 weeks to reach a protective dose, and right now you have no medicine on board and a demonstrated tendency toward convulsions. I recommend a **temporary bridge with levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily (1,000 mg/day, about 15.6 mg/kg/day)**, then tapering it to 250 mg twice daily for 2 weeks and stopping once your lamotrigine level is confirmed. I know that is the drug that upset you. The difference now is that it has a planned end date, we will call you at 2 weeks to check on mood, and if irritability or low mood returns you call us and we change course rather than you stopping alone.

I can try that if it's short. Also, my mom has Lyrica for the nerve pain in her feet from her diabetes. The pharmacist said it's also a seizure medicine. If the Keppra gets bad again, could I just take some of hers instead?

Please don't, and I'm glad you asked before trying it.

**Pregabalin (Lyrica)** is approved for focal seizures only as an **add-on** to another antiseizure medicine, not as a medicine to use on its own, and its seizure effect is modest compared with lamotrigine. It commonly causes dizziness, sleepiness, weight gain and swelling in the legs. Your mother's dose was chosen for her kidneys, her weight and her neuropathy, not for you. Taking it intermittently could make things worse, and stopping it abruptly after regular use can itself provoke seizures.

If levetiracetam becomes intolerable again, call the clinic line. We have several alternatives, and we would rather change your plan within a day than have you improvise. The rule for everything in your cabinet is simple: take only what is prescribed to you, and tell us before starting anything new, including over-the-counter sleep aids and herbal products.
Understood. What about driving and work? And my mom mostly speaks Spanish. She lives with us and she's scared to death after all this. I don't know how to explain it to her.

**Driving:** you should not drive for now. In Texas, the usual standard is six months free of seizures that impair awareness or control before driving is reconsidered, and the Department of Public Safety Medical Advisory Board can review individual cases. Your auras with preserved awareness are handled differently from the spells where you lose awareness, and we will document that distinction for you as your seizures come under control.

**Work:** desk work as a bookkeeper is safe. Tell your manager what a seizure looks like and what to do; you have legal protections under the ADA if you need scheduling adjustments, such as avoiding overnight work during quarter-end.

**Home safety:** shower rather than bathe, with the bathroom door unlocked; no swimming alone; cook on the back burners; and avoid heights such as ladders until you have been seizure-free for a good stretch.

**Seizure first aid for your family:** stay calm, time it, turn you onto your side, put something soft under your head, nothing in your mouth, and call 911 if a convulsion lasts **more than 5 minutes**, if a second one follows before you wake up, or if you are injured or have trouble breathing.

For your mother, I'd like to do this properly. My own Spanish is fine for clinic conversation but not good enough for something this important, so I will book a certified medical interpreter and we can have a session together, you, your husband and your mother, either in person or by video. We also have written seizure first-aid and medication guides in Spanish. I grew up watching my parents, who learned English as adults, have their children translate at doctor visits, and I know how much gets lost and how much weight that puts on the child. You should not have to be the translator for your own diagnosis.
Thank you, that would really help her. What happens if the lamotrigine doesn't work? My cousin has been on like four different medicines.

That is a realistic concern, and I'd rather plan for it now than surprise you later.

Most people with newly diagnosed epilepsy become seizure-free on the first or second well-chosen medication. Mesial temporal sclerosis does carry a higher-than-average chance of **drug-resistant epilepsy**, which the ILAE defines as failure of **two** appropriately chosen, tolerated and adequately dosed medication trials to achieve sustained seizure freedom. We will not wait years to act on that.

If seizures continue after a proper lamotrigine trial and one other medicine, I would bring you in for a **presurgical evaluation**: video-EEG monitoring in our unit to record your typical seizures, neuropsychological testing of memory and language, and additional imaging. For people with unilateral mesial temporal sclerosis whose seizures and testing all point to one hippocampus, surgery, either an anterior temporal lobectomy or a minimally invasive laser ablation, offers a substantially better chance of seizure freedom than trying medication after medication. I'm not predicting that you will need it. I want you to know it exists, and that the next step after two failed medicines is an evaluation, not more years of the same.

To make those decisions well, please keep a **seizure diary**: date, time, type (aura only, staring spell, or convulsion), what preceded it, and any missed doses. Your phone's notes app is fine.
Okay. Is there anything I can do on my own besides the pills? And what do I do if I forget a dose?

Several things make a real difference.

- **Sleep:** your big seizure followed three nights of four hours' sleep. Aim for 7-9 hours with a consistent schedule, and treat quarter-end like a medical constraint, not a test of endurance.
- **Alcohol:** an occasional single glass of wine is generally acceptable once you are stable, but avoid heavier drinking, and especially avoid drinking combined with lost sleep. Alcohol withdrawal the following morning lowers the seizure threshold.
- **Consistency:** take your doses at the same times every day. A weekly pill organizer and a phone alarm are simple and effective.
- **Stress and illness:** fever, vomiting and poor sleep during illness can bring out seizures; call us if you cannot keep your medicine down.

**Missed dose:** if you remember within about 6 hours of the scheduled time, take it. If it is closer to the next dose, skip it and resume the usual schedule. Never double up. If you miss more than one day of lamotrigine, call us before restarting, for the rash reason we discussed.

Also, please tell any doctor, dentist or pharmacist that you take lamotrigine, especially before a new antibiotic, hormone change, or any antiseizure medicine given in an emergency, such as phenytoin.
Can you just summarize the whole plan for me so I can show my husband?

Here is the plan.

**Diagnosis:** focal epilepsy, left mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis. Seizure types: focal aware seizures (rising stomach sensation, deja vu, burnt smell), focal impaired awareness seizures (staring, left-hand fumbling), and one focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure 16 days ago, triggered by sleep deprivation.

**Medicines:**
1. **Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily** as a bridge, restarting today. Phone mood check at 2 weeks. Taper to 250 mg twice daily for 2 weeks once your lamotrigine level is confirmed, then stop.
2. **Lamotrigine** 25 mg daily for weeks 1-2; 50 mg daily for weeks 3-4; 50 mg twice daily in week 5; 75 mg twice daily in week 6; **100 mg twice daily from week 7**. Trough level 2 weeks later (target 2.5-15 mcg/mL). Stop and call for any rash.
3. **Folic acid 1 mg daily.**

**Contraception:** referral for a levonorgestrel IUD. If you stay on Sprintec, take active pills continuously and expect a higher lamotrigine dose. Call before stopping any estrogen-containing pill.

**Interactions to remember:** phenytoin lowers lamotrigine by about 40-50%; carbamazepine combined with valproic acid raises the toxic epoxide, causing nausea, double vision and unsteadiness. Do not take your mother's pregabalin.

**Safety:** no driving for now (Texas generally requires six months free of seizures with loss of awareness); shower rather than bathe, no swimming alone; call 911 for a convulsion over 5 minutes or back-to-back seizures. Call 988 or us if mood worsens.

**Follow-up:** phone call at 2 weeks; clinic visit at 10 weeks with the lamotrigine level; interpreter-supported family session within the next month; preconception visit before you try to conceive. Keep a seizure diary. If seizures persist after two appropriate medicines, we move to a presurgical evaluation.

Thank you for being honest about the levetiracetam today. That honesty is what allowed us to build a plan you can actually follow.

common_mistakes.mistake: Labeling a first convulsion as a single provoked or isolated event without asking about prior focal seizures.
common_mistakes.explanation: Many patients with temporal lobe epilepsy have months to years of unrecognized auras (epigastric rising, deja vu, olfactory phenomena) and focal impaired awareness seizures before their first convulsion. Specifically eliciting these establishes a diagnosis of epilepsy under the ILAE practical definition, changes recurrence risk, and justifies treatment and driving restrictions.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing valproic acid for a woman of childbearing potential with focal epilepsy.
common_mistakes.explanation: Valproate carries a roughly 10% major malformation risk plus dose-dependent neurodevelopmental harm, and it is not the preferred agent for focal epilepsy. Lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred; valproate should be reserved for situations where other options have failed, with a formal pregnancy prevention plan.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring the bidirectional interaction between lamotrigine and estrogen-containing contraceptives.
common_mistakes.explanation: Ethinyl estradiol roughly halves lamotrigine levels during active pills, with rebound during the placebo week; stopping the pill can double levels. Failure to anticipate this causes breakthrough seizures or toxicity. Continuous pill dosing, a levonorgestrel IUD and trough-level monitoring prevent it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Titrating lamotrigine too quickly or restarting at full dose after a prolonged gap.
common_mistakes.explanation: Rapid escalation, co-administration with valproate, and restarting at maintenance dose after roughly five half-lives off drug all increase the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. The initial schedule must reflect co-medications: halved with valproate, doubled with enzyme inducers such as phenytoin or carbamazepine.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming nonadherence reflects indifference instead of screening for levetiracetam psychiatric adverse effects.
common_mistakes.explanation: Irritability, depression and emotional lability are common with levetiracetam and are a frequent cause of silent discontinuation. An undetectable level should prompt a nonjudgmental conversation, suicide risk screening, and a regimen change rather than a simple instruction to take the drug.

differential_diagnosis.differentiating_factors: Typically prolonged, waxing-waning movements, side-to-side head shaking, pelvic thrusting, eyes closed during the event, and rapid return to baseline without post-ictal confusion. Lactate and prolactin are not elevated; video-EEG shows no ictal correlate. In this case, post-ictal aphasia, a lateral tongue bite, transient lactic acidosis, elevated prolactin, and concordant EEG and MRI findings argue against it.

Preceded by orthostatic stress, warmth, nausea or pallor; myoclonic jerks are brief (under 15 to 30 seconds); recovery is rapid with little confusion; lateral tongue biting and prolonged post-ictal aphasia are uncommon. Epigastric auras, deja vu and automatisms are not features of syncope.

Build over minutes with dyspnea, palpitations, paresthesias and fear, last longer than typical auras, and do not produce impaired awareness with automatisms or post-ictal word-finding difficulty. Ictal fear from amygdala involvement is abrupt, stereotyped and brief, and may be followed by staring or automatisms.

Occurs within a close temporal relationship to an acute brain insult or systemic derangement such as hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, or stimulant toxicity. Here glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, alcohol level and drug screen were all unremarkable, and the history of recurrent spontaneous focal seizures excludes a purely provoked event.

differential_diagnosis.condition: Transient global amnesia or migraine aura
differential_diagnosis.differentiating_factors: Transient global amnesia causes hours of anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning but preserved identity and no automatisms. Migraine aura evolves over 5 to 60 minutes with positive visual phenomena and is usually followed by headache, unlike brief stereotyped epigastric and deja vu auras lasting under a minute.

related_diseases.relationship: Prolonged febrile seizures, especially febrile status epilepticus, are strongly associated with later hippocampal sclerosis and mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, often after a latent period of years.

Depression is more common in people with epilepsy, particularly temporal lobe epilepsy, and can be precipitated or worsened by antiseizure medications such as levetiracetam; routine screening is recommended.

A potential life-threatening complication of epilepsy, defined operationally as a convulsive seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery between them; requires emergency treatment.
The leading epilepsy-related cause of death in young adults; the strongest modifiable risk factor is frequent uncontrolled generalized or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
Long-term therapy with enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications such as phenytoin and carbamazepine, and with valproate, is associated with reduced bone mineral density and fracture risk.

original.executive_summary:
## Epilepsy: left mesial temporal lobe epilepsy in a woman of childbearing potential

**Presentation:** 27-year-old right-handed woman seen 16 days after a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure triggered by sleep deprivation; history uncovers a year of focal aware seizures (epigastric rising, deja vu, burnt-rubber smell) and focal impaired awareness seizures with left-hand automatisms, right-arm dystonic posturing and post-ictal aphasia, plus a prolonged febrile seizure at 18 months.

**Key data:** post-ictal ABG pH 7.25 / PaCO2 44 mmHg / HCO3 18.5 mEq/L (mixed lactic and respiratory acidosis), anion gap 19 with lactate 5.9 mmol/L normalizing within 2 hours; prolactin 52 ng/mL; normal glucose, sodium, calcium and toxicology. EEG: left anterior temporal sharp waves and rhythmic slowing. MRI: left hippocampal sclerosis. Levetiracetam level undetectable, revealing concealed discontinuation due to mood effects.

**Diagnosis:** focal epilepsy of structural etiology (ILAE practical definition, PMID: 24730690; ILAE 2017 seizure classification, PMID: 28276060).

**Management:** lamotrigine as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy (SANAD II, PMID: 33838757), titrated from 25 mg daily to 100 mg twice daily (about 3.1 mg/kg/day at 64 kg) with trough-level monitoring; time-limited levetiracetam bridge with mood follow-up; valproate avoided for teratogenicity; carbamazepine and phenytoin avoided as enzyme inducers. Counseling covered the estrogen-lamotrigine interaction (levonorgestrel IUD preferred), phenytoin lowering lamotrigine by 40-50%, the carbamazepine-valproate epoxide interaction, folic acid, rash warning signs, driving restriction, seizure first aid, SUDEP, and early presurgical referral if two appropriate medications fail.

facts.answer: Levodopu beru v sedm ráno, v jednu a v sedm večer. Zabere asi za čtyřicet minut, ale po třech hodinách se třes a pomalost vrací.
facts.sourceText: I take one and a half Sinemet at 7 in the morning, 1 in the afternoon, and 7 at night. It kicks in after maybe 40 minutes. facts.answer: Musím být upřímný: pět měsíců hraju online automaty a na kartě je skoro 9 000 dolarů. Nedokázal jsem přestat, přestože jsem dřív nikdy nehrál.
facts.guardedAnswer: Ne, v hraní ani utrácení se nic nezměnilo.
facts.disclosureReason: Cítil silný stud kvůli dluhům a ztrátě kontroly.
facts.sourceText: Okay. I was not honest before, I am sorry. It is an online slots app. It started maybe five months ago, just a few dollars. Then I was playing every night. Joanna saw the credit card statement: almost nine thousand dollars. I felt so ashamed. I kept telling myself I would stop, and I could not. I have never been a gambler my whole life, Doctor. I worked 34 years and never even went to the casino with the guys.
facts.guardedSourceText: Ernesto 'Ernie' Dimaculangan is a 68-year-old Filipino-American man, a retired civilian aircraft maintenance mechanic, diagnosed with Parkinson's disease six years ago after a left-hand rest tremor began at age 62. He takes carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg 1.5 tablets three times daily, pramipexole 1 mg three times daily, and selegiline 5 mg twice daily. He presents to scheduled follow-up with end-of-dose wearing-off about 3 hours after each dose, two months of visual hallucinations with retained insight, dream-enactment behavior, orthostatic lightheadedness, constipation, and worsening stiffness since an urgent care clinician prescribed metoclopramide for nausea three weeks ago. He initially denies any gambling or spending changes, then acknowledges about 9,000 dollars in online slot-machine losses over five months.

original.name: Parkinson's disease
original.description: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, resulting in motor features including resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability. Non-motor features include cognitive decline, depression, autonomic dysfunction, and sleep disturbances. Treatment is primarily symptomatic with levodopa-based therapies; there is no cure.

drug_interactions.description: Metoclopramide antagonizes the therapeutic effect of levodopa by blocking dopamine receptors and can worsen Parkinson's symptoms.
Combination of selegiline (MAO-B inhibitor) with SSRIs can precipitate serotonin syndrome.
Typical antipsychotics block dopamine receptors and directly counteract levodopa's mechanism, worsening parkinsonism.
