original.prevalence: Overall urticaria lifetime prevalence 15-25%; dermographism affects 2-5% of the population; cold urticaria in 0.05%; cholinergic urticaria 0.2%; inducible urticaria represents 25-45% of all chronic urticaria presentations.
original.clinician_persona: Dr. Ingrid Solberg, MD, is a board-certified allergist-immunologist who runs the chronic urticaria and angioedema clinic at an academic medical center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, where she sees referred patients with refractory spontaneous and inducible urticaria and administers biologic therapy.
original.patient_scenario: Jason Liang (Liang Jiahao), a 31-year-old Chinese-American man who works as a warehouse operations supervisor and operates a forklift for part of most shifts, is referred by his primary care physician for eight months of itchy linear welts that appear within minutes wherever his skin is scratched, rubbed, or pressed by his safety harness, belt, and backpack straps. He is otherwise healthy, weighs 74 kg, and has been using over-the-counter diphenhydramine at night along with cetirizine that his primary care physician prescribed.

conversation.content: This is an outpatient allergy-immunology consultation at an academic chronic urticaria clinic. The clinician is Dr. Ingrid Solberg, allergist-immunologist. The patient is Jason Liang, a 31-year-old man referred for suspected symptomatic dermographism (chronic inducible urticaria, ICD-10 L50.3). The clinician should take a focused history, interpret provocation testing and laboratory results, explain the stepwise guideline approach to treatment, dose medications correctly for the patient's weight of 74 kg where relevant, counsel on drug interactions, and verify medication adherence.

Hi, Dr. Solberg. Thanks for fitting me in. My primary care doctor thinks this is some kind of hives, but honestly I don't know what's going on. Anywhere I scratch, I get these raised red lines that itch like crazy, and they look like someone wrote on me.

I'm glad you came in, Mr. Liang. What you're describing, raised itchy lines that trace exactly where the skin was scratched, is very characteristic, but I'd like to hear the whole story before I put a label on it. When did this start, and what was going on in your life or health around that time?

Please, just Jason. It started around January, so about eight months ago. I had a bad cold right after New Year's, the kind where I was out of work for four days. A couple of weeks after that I noticed welts under my belt line and where my backpack straps sit. Now it's everywhere. At work I wear a safety harness when I'm up on the order picker, and by the end of a shift my shoulders and hips are covered in stripes.

Thank you, Jason. A few specific questions, because the details help separate the different types of urticaria.

1. How quickly do the welts appear after the skin is rubbed, and how long does each one last?
2. Do you ever get hives in places nobody touched, for example waking up with welts on your back or thighs?
3. Have you had any swelling of the lips, eyelids, tongue, or throat, or any trouble breathing or swallowing?
4. Do cold, heat, sweating, exercise, sunlight, or sustained pressure, such as a deep red swelling that appears hours after sitting on a hard chair, set anything off?

They come up in maybe two or three minutes, itch the most in the first ten minutes, and are gone within about half an hour. I don't think I get them out of nowhere; it's always somewhere that got rubbed, though sometimes I don't notice I scratched until I see the line. No swelling in my face or throat, never had trouble breathing. Hot showers make me itchy, but I think that's because I towel off hard afterward. Cold doesn't bother me, and I play pickup basketball without getting the little dot-type hives.

That's a very clear history. Wheals that appear within minutes of friction, last under an hour, stay confined to rubbed skin, and occur without spontaneous hives or angioedema point strongly toward **symptomatic dermographism**, which is the most common form of chronic inducible urticaria. The timing after a viral illness is also typical; we often cannot identify a single cause, but an infection preceding onset is a frequent story.

I also want to make sure we are not missing a second process. Some people have dermographism alongside chronic spontaneous urticaria, and the absence of pinpoint hives with basketball makes cholinergic urticaria less likely. Now, about treatment so far. What are you taking, how often, and what dose?

My doctor prescribed cetirizine, 10 mg, and I take it every morning. It's been about ten weeks. It takes the edge off, but I still get welts every day. At night the itching keeps me up, so I take Benadryl, usually two of the 25 mg pills, before bed. That knocks me out, but I feel groggy in the morning.

Thank you for telling me about the Benadryl, because that matters for your safety. Two 25 mg tablets is **50 mg of diphenhydramine**, which for your weight of 74 kg works out to about **0.68 mg/kg**. That is within the usual adult nonprescription range, but diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine. It crosses into the brain, its sedating and anticholinergic effects persist well into the next morning, and driving studies show it impairs performance even when people feel alert, with effects that can carry into the next morning. Since you operate a forklift and an order picker, the morning grogginess is a genuine workplace hazard, not just an inconvenience. Current international urticaria guidelines advise against routine use of first-generation antihistamines for exactly this reason.

Before I examine you and review the results, let me go back to the cetirizine. You mentioned taking it every morning for ten weeks. Your primary care physician sent the prescription for a 30-tablet supply, and the pharmacy record I have shows it was filled once, ten weeks ago, with no refills. Help me reconcile that. Did you get more from somewhere else, or has it been more of an as-needed routine?

Okay, that's fair. I didn't buy more. I take it on days when I know I'll be in the harness, or when it's really bad. So maybe three or four days a week. I figured if I took it every day my body would get used to it and it would stop working. Also, my mom thinks I shouldn't be on medicine every day for a skin thing. She had me cutting out mango and fried foods because she says they're too heaty. I didn't want to sound like I wasn't following the plan.

I appreciate you telling me, and it's a very common pattern, so there's no judgment here. It actually helps me, because it changes what the next step should be.

Two points. First, second-generation antihistamines like cetirizine do not lose effectiveness with daily use; there is no tolerance effect in urticaria. They work best as a **regular daily preventive**, because they keep histamine receptors occupied before mast cells release histamine. Taking a dose only after welts are already out gives you much less benefit. So what looked like a partial failure of cetirizine is really an incomplete trial of it.

Second, about the food changes: it was thoughtful of your mother to look for a trigger, and many families have food-based approaches to skin problems. In dermographism, though, the trigger is mechanical friction on the skin, and there is no evidence that food avoidance helps. Since cutting out mango and fried food hasn't changed anything over these months, you can eat normally. That may make home life easier, and it keeps us from chasing a trigger that isn't there.

Let me go over your exam and testing now.
Sure. The nurse did some kind of scratch test on my back with a little plastic comb thing. I stopped the cetirizine three days ago like your office told me to.

Good, that washout was important, because antihistamines suppress the test and can produce a false negative.

Your vital signs today: **BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.8 °C, SpO2 99% on room air.** Weight **74 kg**, height **175 cm**, which gives a **BMI of 24.2 kg/m²**.

On examination there were no spontaneous wheals and no angioedema. Your oropharynx, lungs, and joints were normal, and there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Stroking your upper back with a tongue depressor produced linear, raised wheals with surrounding flare within about 3 minutes, which we call a positive dermographism sign.

The plastic device was a **FricTest**, a standardized four-pin friction tool. The pins apply increasing pressure, and the number of pins that produce a wheal estimates your trigger threshold. You reacted to **3 of 4 pins** at the 10-minute reading, meaning a low threshold and fairly sensitive skin. This standardized provocation testing follows the international consensus on diagnosing chronic inducible urticaria (PMID: 26991006), and it gives us a baseline to measure your response to treatment.

You also completed the **Urticaria Control Test**, a four-question score from 0 to 16 where 12 or higher means well controlled. Your score was **5 of 16**, so your urticaria is poorly controlled at present.
Makes sense. What about the blood work? My doctor ran a bunch of stuff before I came here.

Your results are reassuring, and I'll go through them with reference ranges.

**Complete blood count:** WBC **6.8 x10^9/L** (4.0 to 11.0), eosinophils **0.2 x10^9/L** (0.0 to 0.5), hemoglobin **15.1 g/dL** (13.5 to 17.5), platelets **248 x10^9/L** (150 to 400).

**Inflammatory markers:** CRP **1.2 mg/L** (under 5.0), ESR **6 mm/h** (0 to 15).

**Thyroid:** TSH **1.9 mIU/L** (0.4 to 4.0), anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies **8 IU/mL** (under 35).

**Total IgE:** **142 IU/mL** (reference 0 to 100). That is mildly elevated, which is common in people with allergic tendencies and is not a problem here. If we ever need omalizumab, a normal or elevated total IgE tends to predict a better response than a very low level.

**Basic metabolic panel:** sodium **139 mmol/L** (135 to 145), potassium **4.1 mmol/L** (3.5 to 5.1), chloride **103 mmol/L** (98 to 107), bicarbonate **25 mmol/L** (22 to 29), giving an **anion gap of 11 mmol/L** (139 minus 103 minus 25; reference 8 to 16). BUN **14 mg/dL** (7 to 20), creatinine **0.9 mg/dL** (0.7 to 1.3), glucose **92 mg/dL** (70 to 99).

Nothing here suggests an underlying systemic illness, infection, or autoimmune thyroid disease. Normal CRP and ESR also argue against urticarial vasculitis, in which individual lesions last more than 24 hours and leave bruising. For isolated dermographism, the guidelines do not recommend broader testing such as allergy panels or food IgE testing, because they do not change management.
So what's the plan? Do I just have to live with this?

No. Most people with dermographism can be brought to good control, and in many it fades on its own over a few years. The treatment approach follows the international EAACI/GA²LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI guideline (PMID: 34536239), which uses a stepwise plan:

**Step 1: Daily second-generation antihistamine at standard dose.** Restart **cetirizine 10 mg once daily, every day**, including days off work and good days. Adult dosing is fixed and not weight-based; at 74 kg you take the standard adult dose.

**Step 2: Up-dose if not controlled after 2 to 4 weeks.** Increase to **cetirizine 10 mg twice daily (20 mg/day)**, and if needed to **20 mg twice daily (40 mg/day)**, which is four times the label dose. This is an off-label use, but the guideline specifically recommends it because it helps many people who fail the standard dose, and the safety record at these doses is good.

**If cetirizine is too sedating** (some people are sensitive to it even though it is a second-generation drug), we switch to **desloratadine (Aerius) 5 mg once daily**, which can be up-dosed the same way to a maximum of **20 mg/day**. Desloratadine is generally less sedating.

**Step 3: Omalizumab if still uncontrolled after 2 to 4 weeks at the 4-fold dose.** I'll explain that option in detail if we reach it.

From today I'd like you to **stop the nightly diphenhydramine**. Once you take cetirizine consistently, the nighttime itch usually improves substantially. If you need extra coverage at night, the preferred approach is to take the second cetirizine dose in the evening, not to add Benadryl.
Won't I be sleepy at work if I take four times the cetirizine?

That's a reasonable concern given your job. Cetirizine causes somnolence in a minority of people, and the risk rises modestly at higher doses. A few precautions:

1. When you move to twice-daily dosing, take the first extra dose on a day off to see how you feel before operating equipment.
2. If you notice drowsiness, reaction slowing, or difficulty concentrating, do not drive or operate the forklift, and call us. We would switch you to desloratadine rather than push through it.
3. Avoid alcohol on the higher dose, because it adds to any sedation.

On the medication side, I also want to check a couple of things. Are you on any antidepressants or mood medications, including older ones called MAO inhibitors such as phenelzine or tranylcypromine, or a selegiline skin patch? And have you taken any antibiotics recently?
No antidepressants. I'm allergic to penicillin, so when I get strep throat my doctor usually gives me erythromycin. I had it maybe last spring. Nothing right now.

Thanks, that's useful to know in advance.

**Erythromycin and desloratadine:** Erythromycin inhibits the liver enzyme CYP3A4 and modestly raises desloratadine levels. In the studies that looked at this, the increase did not cause clinically meaningful effects, including no change in the heart's electrical conduction, so it is a **minor interaction**. If you need erythromycin while on desloratadine, you would not have to stop or change the dose. Just make sure the prescriber knows your full medication list.

I asked about MAO inhibitors because of a medication we sometimes use later in the treatment sequence, **doxepin**. Doxepin is an older tricyclic antidepressant, but at low doses it is one of the most potent H1 and H2 antihistamines available, and some urticaria patients use a small bedtime dose, **10 to 25 mg at night**, for stubborn nocturnal itch. It is not first-line. It is sedating, has anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and constipation, and can prolong the QT interval, so we would get an ECG first.

The critical warning is this: **doxepin must never be combined with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor**, or started within 14 days of stopping one. The combination can cause dangerously high body temperature, seizures, and potentially fatal serotonin syndrome. MAO-inhibiting activity also shows up in unexpected places: the antibiotic **linezolid** and the dye **methylene blue** used in some surgeries both act as MAO inhibitors. If doxepin ever becomes part of your regimen, every clinician who treats you, including in an emergency department or before surgery, needs to know.
Okay. And the omalizumab thing, what is that exactly? Is that a shot?

Yes. **Omalizumab (Xolair)** is a monoclonal antibody that binds free IgE, which leads to fewer IgE receptors on mast cells and makes those cells much less prone to release histamine in response to triggers like friction.

**Dosing:** For urticaria it is **300 mg by subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks**. Unlike its use in asthma, the urticaria dose is **not calculated from body weight or IgE level**, so your 74 kg and IgE of 142 IU/mL don't change it. We would reassess after 3 to 6 months.

**Evidence in your condition:** Omalizumab is approved for chronic spontaneous urticaria. For symptomatic dermographism specifically it is used off-label, but it has been tested in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial (PMID: 28389391). In that study of patients whose dermographism was not controlled by antihistamines, significantly more patients on omalizumab than on placebo became completely free of friction-induced wheals on the FricTest after 10 weeks, roughly half on the 300 mg dose versus about one in ten on placebo. Because it's off-label, insurers usually require documentation that antihistamine up-dosing failed, which is another reason a clean, consistent trial of daily cetirizine matters.

**Safety:** It is generally well tolerated. The main risk is **anaphylaxis, which is rare, roughly 1 to 2 per 1,000 patients**, and can occur even after several uneventful doses. For that reason we give the first injections here with observation afterward, and we prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector for you to carry on injection days. Injection-site reactions and headache are the most common side effects.
I'd rather not do shots if I can avoid it. Is there anything else I can do in the meantime, like at work?

Trigger reduction is a real part of treatment for inducible urticaria, and it's worth doing alongside the medication.

1. **Harness and straps:** Ask about padded shoulder and leg straps for your harness, and wear a snug, smooth, moisture-wicking base layer so the harness doesn't rub bare skin. Wider backpack straps spread pressure.
2. **Clothing:** Choose soft fabrics, avoid rough seams or wool against the skin, and loosen your belt a notch.
3. **After showers:** Pat dry rather than toweling hard, and use lukewarm water.
4. **Itch without scratching:** Scratching creates new welts and keeps the itch going. A cool compress, or pressing firmly on the itchy area rather than scratching, usually works better.
5. **Moisturize:** Dry skin itches more; a fragrance-free emollient once or twice a day helps.

If you'd like, I can write a brief letter for your employer about harness modifications. It won't disclose details beyond what you choose to share.
That letter would help, actually. My supervisor keeps asking why I'm always scratching. How long until I know if the daily cetirizine is working?

I'll have the letter ready before you leave.

You should notice improvement within the first week of truly daily dosing, but we judge each step over **2 to 4 weeks**. Here's the concrete timeline:

- **Today:** Restart cetirizine 10 mg every morning. Stop diphenhydramine.
- **Week 2:** If welts still appear most days or the itch disturbs sleep, go to 10 mg twice daily. Our nurse will call to check in, and you can message us any time.
- **Week 4:** If still uncontrolled, go to 20 mg twice daily.
- **Week 6 to 8 visit:** We repeat the FricTest and the Urticaria Control Test. A UCT of 12 or more and fewer positive pins would mean you're controlled. If you are still not controlled on 40 mg/day, we talk about omalizumab, with a low bedtime dose of doxepin as a possible additional option for night symptoms if you want to avoid injections a bit longer.

Please keep a simple log: the date, your cetirizine doses, and a 0 to 10 itch score each evening. Photos of welts are helpful too. Most importantly, if you ever develop swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, or lightheadedness, that is not typical of dermographism and needs emergency care; call 911.
Got it. One more thing: my mom is going to ask if this is contagious or if my kids could get it someday. I don't have kids yet, but she worries.

Those are fair questions, and you can tell her:

**It is not contagious.** Dermographism comes from mast cells in your own skin being overly sensitive to mechanical triggers. It cannot pass to anyone through contact, sharing towels, or anything else.

**It is not considered hereditary in any simple way.** People with allergic conditions in the family may have a slightly higher tendency toward urticaria in general, but there is no specific gene test, and your future children would not be expected to inherit dermographism.

**It usually improves over time.** Many people see it become much milder or resolve within several years, though timing is hard to predict. Treatment keeps you comfortable in the meantime and doesn't change the natural course.

If she'd like to come to a future visit, she's welcome. Sometimes hearing it directly makes it easier to accept daily medication.
Thanks. I think I underestimated how much taking it on and off was messing this up. I'll take it every day and bring the log.

That sounds like a solid plan, and thank you again for being honest about the dosing. It changed my recommendation from escalating treatment to first giving the standard dose a fair trial.

To summarize:

1. **Diagnosis:** Symptomatic dermographism (chronic inducible urticaria), confirmed with a FricTest positive at **3 of 4 pins**; UCT **5 of 16**; normal CBC, CRP, ESR, TSH, and chemistry.
2. **Now:** **Cetirizine 10 mg daily**, every day. **Stop diphenhydramine** because of next-day sedation and the risk while operating equipment.
3. **Escalation:** Cetirizine up to **40 mg/day** in 2 to 4 week steps; switch to **desloratadine 5 to 20 mg/day** if sedated.
4. **If refractory:** **Omalizumab 300 mg SC every 4 weeks**, with observation and an epinephrine auto-injector; low-dose **doxepin** at bedtime only after an ECG and with strict avoidance of MAO inhibitors, linezolid, and methylene blue.
5. **Interactions:** Erythromycin with desloratadine is minor and needs no change.
6. **Trigger reduction:** Padded harness straps, a smooth base layer, patting dry, pressing instead of scratching.
7. **Follow-up:** Nurse call at 2 weeks, clinic visit with repeat FricTest and UCT at 6 to 8 weeks. Emergency care for any throat, tongue, or breathing symptoms.

I'll print the plan and the employer letter for you at checkout.

common_mistakes.mistake: Labeling an antihistamine trial as a failure without verifying daily adherence
common_mistakes.explanation: Second-generation H1-antihistamines work as daily preventives; intermittent, as-needed use gives markedly less control. Escalating to up-dosing or biologics before confirming consistent daily use leads to unnecessary off-label therapy and insurance denials. Refill history and a direct, nonjudgmental question often reveal the gap.

common_mistakes.mistake: Relying on first-generation sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine for maintenance or nighttime control
common_mistakes.explanation: Current urticaria guidelines advise against routine first-generation H1-antihistamine use because of next-day sedation, psychomotor and driving impairment, and anticholinergic effects, often without the patient feeling impaired. The correct escalation is up-dosing a second-generation agent up to fourfold, with the extra dose taken in the evening if nighttime itch predominates.

common_mistakes.mistake: Performing provocation testing without an antihistamine washout, or skipping standardized testing altogether
common_mistakes.explanation: Antihistamines suppress the wheal response and can produce a false-negative FricTest or dermographometer result. Consensus recommendations call for stopping antihistamines for several days before testing. Standardized threshold testing also provides a baseline for objectively measuring response to treatment.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ordering extensive laboratory workups, food allergy panels, or recommending elimination diets for isolated dermographism
common_mistakes.explanation: In symptomatic dermographism the trigger is mechanical friction, and there is no evidence that food avoidance helps. Broad allergy panels and food-specific IgE testing do not change management and can create false positives that lead to needless dietary restriction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dosing omalizumab for urticaria by body weight and total IgE, as in asthma
common_mistakes.explanation: For chronic urticaria, omalizumab is given as a fixed 300 mg subcutaneous dose every 4 weeks (150 mg is an alternative in some regions) regardless of weight or IgE. Using the asthma dosing table leads to incorrect doses. Patients also need anaphylaxis counseling, observation after early doses, and an epinephrine auto-injector.

differential_diagnosis.differentiating_factors: Wheals and/or angioedema appear without a consistent physical trigger, including on unrubbed skin, often with nocturnal or morning predominance. Dermographism wheals are strictly linear or confined to friction sites and are reproduced by FricTest or dermographometer. The two conditions can coexist, so ask specifically about spontaneous hives.

Deep, painful or burning swellings appear 30 minutes to 12 hours after sustained vertical pressure (straps, sitting, walking) and last 12 to 72 hours, sometimes with malaise. Symptomatic dermographism wheals appear within minutes of shearing friction and resolve in under an hour. Diagnosis uses weighted-rod testing with delayed readings.

Small punctate (1 to 3 mm) wheals with large flares triggered by a rise in core body temperature from exercise, hot showers, emotional stress, or spicy food, not by friction. Confirmed by exercise or passive warming provocation. Linear friction-induced wheals argue for dermographism.

Individual lesions persist more than 24 hours, burn more than itch, and resolve with purpura or hyperpigmentation. Often accompanied by arthralgia, elevated ESR/CRP, and in the hypocomplementemic form low C3/C4. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Transient wheals lasting under an hour with normal inflammatory markers argue against it.

Fixed red-brown macules or papules that urticate when rubbed (positive Darier sign), in contrast to dermographism, where wheals arise on normal-appearing skin. Serum tryptase may be elevated and systemic symptoms such as flushing or anaphylaxis may occur. Diagnosed by skin biopsy, with tryptase and bone marrow evaluation when indicated.

related_diseases.relationship: Shares the mast cell-driven mechanism and the same stepwise treatment algorithm (second-generation antihistamines, up-dosing, omalizumab, cyclosporine). A substantial minority of chronic spontaneous urticaria patients also have an inducible component, most often dermographism.

Another chronic inducible urticaria subtype, triggered by cold contact. It carries a risk of systemic reactions and anaphylaxis with cold-water immersion. Diagnosed by ice-cube or TempTest provocation and treated with the same antihistamine up-dosing approach.

Chronic inducible urticaria triggered by increased core body temperature. It can coexist with dermographism in the same patient and is managed with trigger modification and the standard antihistamine step-up.

Atopic patients commonly show dermographism and elevated total IgE. However, atopic dermatitis produces persistent eczematous plaques rather than transient wheals, and it may coexist with urticaria and complicate assessment of itch.

Bradykinin-mediated angioedema occurs without wheals and does not respond to antihistamines or omalizumab. It must be distinguished from mast cell-mediated urticaria with angioedema by testing C4 and C1-inhibitor levels and function when angioedema occurs without hives.

original.executive_summary:
## Symptomatic Dermographism (Chronic Inducible Urticaria, L50.3)

**Presentation:** A 31-year-old warehouse supervisor has 8 months of friction-induced linear wheals that appear within 2 to 3 minutes and resolve within 30 minutes, beginning after a viral illness, with no spontaneous hives or angioedema.

**Diagnosis:** FricTest positive at **3 of 4 pins** after a 3-day antihistamine washout; Urticaria Control Test **5/16** (poorly controlled). CBC, CRP **1.2 mg/L**, ESR **6 mm/h**, TSH, anti-TPO, and chemistry (anion gap **11 mmol/L**) are normal; total IgE **142 IU/mL**.

**Key finding:** The apparent cetirizine failure reflected intermittent, as-needed use (a 30-tablet fill once in 10 weeks), which was caught tactfully through refill history. The patient was also taking diphenhydramine 50 mg (0.68 mg/kg) nightly, causing next-day sedation while operating a forklift.

**Plan (guideline stepwise):** Daily cetirizine 10 mg, up-dosed to 40 mg/day over 2 to 4 week intervals; desloratadine 5 to 20 mg/day if sedated; stop diphenhydramine; omalizumab 300 mg SC every 4 weeks (fixed dose, off-label for dermographism, RCT-supported) if refractory; bedtime doxepin 10 to 25 mg as a later option after an ECG, with strict avoidance of MAOIs, linezolid, and methylene blue. Erythromycin with desloratadine is a minor CYP3A4 interaction needing no adjustment. Trigger reduction includes padded harness straps and avoiding scratching. Repeat FricTest and UCT at 6 to 8 weeks.

cases.title: Pokles nálady a ztráta zájmů
cases.opening: Několik týdnů se z ničeho netěším a v práci dělám chyby, které jsem dřív nedělal.

facts.topic: Délka obtíží, anhedonie a funkční dopad
facts.answer: Asi deset týdnů. Přestal jsem hrát fotbal i na kytaru s dcerou. V práci jsem přehlédl dvě chyby a pořád si to vyčítám.
facts.sourceText: It started maybe ten weeks ago, around the end of the big pipeline project. I wake up at 3:30 or 4 every morning and can't get back to sleep. I'm not hungry, I've lost about 4 kilos without trying. I used to play in a Sunday soccer league and play guitar with my daughter; I quit the league and the guitar just sits there. At work I missed two errors in a spec review last month that I would normally catch in my sleep. I keep replaying it. I feel like I'm letting everybody down.

facts.topic: Spánek, chuť k jídlu a hmotnost
facts.answer: Budím se kolem půl čtvrté nebo čtvrté a neusnu. Nemám hlad a zhubnul jsem čtyři kila.
facts.sourceText: It started maybe ten weeks ago, around the end of the big pipeline project. I wake up at 3:30 or 4 every morning and can't get back to sleep. I'm not hungry, I've lost about 4 kilos without trying. I used to play in a Sunday soccer league and play guitar with my daughter; I quit the league and the guitar just sits there. At work I missed two errors in a spec review last month that I would normally catch in my sleep. I keep replaying it. I feel like I'm letting everybody down.

facts.answer: Někdy si ráno říkám, že by bylo snazší se neprobudit. Dcera je důvod, proč si nechci nic udělat.
facts.sourceText: Mornings are the worst. By evening I'm a little more functional. My wife says I talk slower, and I do feel like I'm moving through mud. As for the other thing... sometimes lying awake at 4 in the morning I think it would be easier to just not wake up. I would never actually do anything. I have my daughter.

facts.topic: Plán, předchozí pokusy a přístup ke zbraním
facts.answer: Žádný plán ani předchozí pokus nemám. Ve skříni v ložnici ale mám loveckou pušku, náboje jsou v garáži.
facts.sourceText: No, no, and no. It's more of a wish to not exist for a while than any kind of plan. Never tried anything, never cut or anything like that. I do have a deer rifle in a case in the bedroom closet. It's not loaded; the ammunition is in the garage.

facts.topic: Neuvedené léky na bolest a jejich skutečné užívání
facts.answer: Před pěti týdny jsem si natáhl záda a dostal tramadol. I když jsou záda lepší, beru většinu nocí jednu až dvě tablety, protože po něm usnu a chvíli se cítím méně prázdný.
facts.guardedAnswer: Žádné další léky pravidelně neužívám.
facts.disclosureReason: Bál se, že bude považován za člověka vyhledávajícího návykové léky.
facts.sourceText: Yeah. Sorry. I pulled my lower back moving a water heater about five or six weeks ago. Urgent care gave me the tramadol. I've been taking one or two at bedtime most nights, even though the back is a lot better. Honestly it helps me sleep, and for a few hours I feel less flat. I didn't mention it because I figured you'd think I was a pill guy.
facts.guardedSourceText: Mateo Callahan is a 34-year-old biracial man (Mexican-American mother from El Paso, Irish-American father from Ohio) who works as a civil engineer and project manager for a municipal water utility. He is married with a 6-year-old daughter and is referred by his primary care physician after roughly ten weeks of low mood, loss of interest, early-morning awakening, reduced appetite with a 4 kg weight loss, and worsening concentration at work; his PHQ-9 in primary care was 19. He has no prior psychiatric treatment, a father who was treated for depression, and a lumbar strain from five weeks ago that he has been managing with medication he initially does not disclose.

original.name: Depression (major depressive disorder)
original.description: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a common and serious mood disorder characterized by persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, changes in sleep, appetite, and energy, cognitive impairment, and feelings of worthlessness lasting at least two weeks. It affects approximately 280 million people worldwide and is a leading cause of disability. Treatment typically involves a combination of antidepressant pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy, with response rates around 50-60% for first-line agents.

original.prevalence: Affects approximately 280 million people worldwide; 12-month prevalence of 7% in the United States; leading cause of disability in middle-income countries; women affected at 1.5-2x the rate of men
original.clinician_persona: Dr. Marisol Villarreal, MD, is a Mexican-American, board-certified adult psychiatrist who leads the collaborative-care behavioral health program embedded in a large family medicine practice in San Antonio, Texas, where she sees referred primary care patients for diagnostic assessment, medication management, and measurement-based follow-up alongside a nurse care manager and staff therapists.
original.patient_scenario: Mateo Callahan is a 34-year-old biracial man (Mexican-American mother from El Paso, Irish-American father from Ohio) who works as a civil engineer and project manager for a municipal water utility. He is married with a 6-year-old daughter and is referred by his primary care physician after roughly ten weeks of low mood, loss of interest, early-morning awakening, reduced appetite with a 4 kg weight loss, and worsening concentration at work; his PHQ-9 in primary care was 19. He has no prior psychiatric treatment, a father who was treated for depression, and a lumbar strain from five weeks ago that he has been managing with medication he initially does not disclose.

conversation.content: You are Dr. Marisol Villarreal, MD, a board-certified adult psychiatrist in an integrated collaborative-care clinic within a family medicine practice in San Antonio, Texas. You are conducting a new-patient psychiatric evaluation and a four-week follow-up for a primary care referral for suspected major depressive disorder. Use a measured, professional, evidence-based style. Assess suicide risk directly, screen for bipolar disorder and substances before prescribing, review the state prescription monitoring program, rule out medical mimics, explain treatment options with accurate dosing and interactions, and use measurement-based care (PHQ-9) to guide dose adjustments. Cite evidence accurately and never overstate what a study found.

Hi. I'm Mateo. Honestly, my wife made this appointment, and Dr. Nguyen pushed me to keep it. I'm not sure I belong in a psychiatrist's office. I've just been in a rut for a couple of months and I figured it would pass.

Thank you for coming in, Mateo. I'm Dr. Villarreal, and I work with Dr. Nguyen's team here. Many people arrive at this office feeling exactly the way you describe, so there is nothing unusual about it. Dr. Nguyen sent me his note and the PHQ-9 questionnaire you completed last week, which scored **19 out of 27**. That range usually reflects more than a rut, so I would like to understand what the past couple of months have actually looked like for you.

Could you walk me through when you first noticed a change, and what a typical day is like now? I am particularly interested in your sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and whether things you used to enjoy still feel enjoyable.

It started maybe ten weeks ago, around the end of the big pipeline project. I wake up at 3:30 or 4 every morning and can't get back to sleep. I'm not hungry, I've lost about 4 kilos without trying. I used to play in a Sunday soccer league and play guitar with my daughter; I quit the league and the guitar just sits there. At work I missed two errors in a spec review last month that I would normally catch in my sleep. I keep replaying it. I feel like I'm letting everybody down.

That is a very clear description, and it maps onto a recognizable pattern. What you are describing includes several of the core features we look for: loss of interest in things that used to matter to you (the soccer league, the guitar), early-morning awakening, reduced appetite with unintended weight loss, trouble concentrating, and a sense of guilt that keeps replaying. When these are present most days for at least two weeks and interfere with work and family life, the diagnosis we consider is major depressive disorder.

A few more specifics will help. Is your mood worse at a particular time of day, for example heaviest in the morning and a little lighter by evening? Do you feel physically slowed down, or the opposite, restless and unable to sit still? And I want to ask something I ask everyone in your situation, directly: in the past month, have you had thoughts that life is not worth living, or that you would be better off dead?

Mornings are the worst. By evening I'm a little more functional. My wife says I talk slower, and I do feel like I'm moving through mud. As for the other thing... sometimes lying awake at 4 in the morning I think it would be easier to just not wake up. I would never actually do anything. I have my daughter.

I appreciate you telling me that. It is a common experience in depression, and saying it out loud is what allows us to keep you safe. I am going to ask a few follow-up questions from a standard screening tool, the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale, so that I understand exactly where you are.

1. Have you had any actual thoughts of killing yourself, beyond wishing you would not wake up?
2. Have you thought about how you might do it?
3. Have you had any intention of acting on those thoughts, or started to prepare in any way?
4. Have you ever tried to hurt yourself or end your life in the past?
5. Are there firearms or large quantities of medication in your home?

No, no, and no. It's more of a wish to not exist for a while than any kind of plan. Never tried anything, never cut or anything like that. I do have a deer rifle in a case in the bedroom closet. It's not loaded; the ammunition is in the garage.

Thank you. Based on your answers, what you are experiencing is passive suicidal ideation: a wish not to be alive, without active thoughts of suicide, a method, intent, or any prior attempts. Your daughter and your wife are clear protective factors. That places you at a lower acute risk, and outpatient treatment is appropriate. It does not make the thoughts trivial, and I want to put some safeguards in place while the depression is active.

The single most effective step is putting time and distance between a person and a lethal method during a rough period. Would you be willing to ask someone you trust to hold the rifle until you are feeling well? Separately storing the ammunition helps, but having the firearm out of the house entirely is better.

We will also write a short safety plan together today: your personal warning signs, what you can do on your own, who you can call, and the **988** Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which you can call or text at any hour. If the thoughts ever shift from wishing you were not here to thinking about acting on it, that is a reason to call 988 or go to an emergency department immediately.

Before we talk about treatment, I need to rule out a condition that can look like depression but is treated very differently. Have you ever had a stretch of days where you needed far less sleep than usual yet felt full of energy, talked faster, took on many projects, or spent money impulsively? And how much alcohol, cannabis, or other substances are you using?

My brother Nico hunts too; he'd hold the rifle for me without asking a lot of questions. I can bring it by his place this weekend. As for the energy stuff, no. I've never been that guy. Even in college I needed my eight hours. I drink maybe two or three beers a week, usually Saturday. No weed, no drugs. My dad was on some antidepressant for a few years after he retired, but nobody in the family has been diagnosed with bipolar or anything like that that I know of.

That is a good plan with Nico, and I would like you to do it before the weekend if you can. A history with no hypomanic or manic episodes and no family history of bipolar disorder makes a unipolar depression much more likely, which matters because antidepressant monotherapy can destabilize bipolar disorder. Your alcohol use is in a low-risk range; your AUDIT-C score works out to **2 to 3**, below the screening threshold of 4 for men. Your father's history of depression is relevant, since having a first-degree relative with depression raises risk.

One more question before I review your results. What medications, over-the-counter products, or supplements are you currently taking, including anything you take only occasionally?
Nothing really. Some ibuprofen now and then for my back. That's it.

Understood. Let me go through today's findings and the labs Dr. Nguyen drew last week.

**Vital signs today:** BP **124/78 mmHg**, HR **72 bpm**, RR **14/min**, temperature **36.7 C**, SpO2 **99%** on room air. Weight **74.0 kg**, height **178 cm**, BMI **23.4 kg/m2**. Your chart shows **78.0 kg** at your physical five months ago (BMI 24.6), so you have lost about **5%** of your body weight.

**Mental status:** well groomed, cooperative, noticeably slowed speech with a pause before answers, mood described as empty, affect constricted and sad, thoughts organized and goal-directed, no hallucinations or delusions, passive death wish without intent or plan, insight and judgment intact. Brief neurological exam and thyroid exam are unremarkable.

**Laboratory results (reference ranges in parentheses):**
- Hemoglobin **14.6 g/dL** (13.5 to 17.5), WBC **6.8 x10^9/L** (4.5 to 11.0), platelets **245 x10^9/L** (150 to 400), MCV **89 fL** (80 to 100)
- Sodium **139 mmol/L** (135 to 145), potassium **4.1 mmol/L** (3.5 to 5.0), chloride **103 mmol/L** (98 to 107), bicarbonate **25 mmol/L** (22 to 29); anion gap 139 minus (103 + 25) = **11 mmol/L** (8 to 12)
- BUN **14 mg/dL** (7 to 20), creatinine **0.96 mg/dL** (0.70 to 1.30), glucose **92 mg/dL** fasting (70 to 99), calcium **9.4 mg/dL** (8.5 to 10.2)
- AST **22 U/L** (10 to 40), ALT **25 U/L** (7 to 56), albumin **4.3 g/dL** (3.5 to 5.0)
- TSH **1.8 mIU/L** (0.4 to 4.0)
- Vitamin B12 **512 pg/mL** (200 to 900), folate **11.2 ng/mL** (greater than 4.0)
- HbA1c **5.2%** (4.0 to 5.6)
- 8 AM total testosterone **486 ng/dL** (264 to 916)
- Urine drug immunoassay: negative for amphetamines, cocaine, cannabinoids, opiates, and benzodiazepines

Your estimated creatinine clearance by Cockcroft-Gault is about **113 mL/min**, so kidney function is normal. In short, there is no thyroid disease, anemia, B12 or folate deficiency, diabetes, low testosterone, or electrolyte problem explaining your symptoms.
So everything is normal. Doesn't that mean this is all in my head, basically? Like I just need to push through it?

Normal labs mean we have ruled out the common medical conditions that imitate depression. They do not mean the depression is imaginary or a matter of willpower. Major depressive disorder is a brain-based illness involving changes in sleep regulation, appetite, stress-hormone signaling, and the circuits that generate motivation and pleasure. The early-morning awakening, weight loss, slowed speech, and morning-worse mood pattern you describe are physiological features; they are the reason we can make this diagnosis with reasonable confidence.

Putting it together, you meet criteria for **major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate to severe, without psychotic features**. Your PHQ-9 score of **19** falls in the moderately severe band (15 to 19), and at this level, guidelines support treatment with an antidepressant, psychotherapy, or ideally both.

Part of it is how I was raised, I think. My mom's side of the family in El Paso would say echarle ganas, just put your back into it and pray. My dad's side, the Callahans, just don't talk about feelings at all. My Spanish isn't great, but I understood the message from both sides: tough it out. So I feel kind of weak sitting here.

I recognize that phrase; my grandmother in Laredo said it to all of us. It usually comes from love and from people who had to get through hard things without many resources. But effort does not fix a depressive episode any more than effort fixes a broken ankle. You have been pushing through for ten weeks, and that is part of why you are exhausted.

It may also help to know how common this is. A Global Burden of Disease analysis estimated about **53 million additional cases** of major depressive disorder worldwide in 2020 alone as a result of the pandemic, an increase of roughly **28%** over expected levels (PMID: 34634250). Men are diagnosed less often than women, in part because they are less likely to report symptoms, which delays treatment. Coming in today is not weakness; it is the step that shortens the illness.

If it would help, I am glad to meet with you and your wife together at some point, or to give you written material you can share with your family, in English or Spanish.
Maybe later. My wife already gets it; she's the one who noticed. Okay, so what are the options? I don't want to be walking around like a zombie at work.

Before we choose, there is one thing I need to raise. Before I prescribe for any new patient, I review the Texas Prescription Monitoring Program, which lists controlled-substance prescriptions filled at any pharmacy. It shows **tramadol 50 mg, 30 tablets**, filled about five weeks ago from an urgent care clinic, and a second fill of **30 tablets** twelve days ago. When I asked about medications, you mentioned only ibuprofen.

I am not raising this to catch you out. People often do not think of a pain prescription as relevant to a psychiatry visit, or feel awkward about how they are using it. It matters a great deal here, because tramadol interacts with several of the antidepressants I am about to recommend, and it also does not show up on the standard urine opiate screen, so I would not have seen it otherwise. Can you tell me how you have actually been taking it?

Yeah. Sorry. I pulled my lower back moving a water heater about five or six weeks ago. Urgent care gave me the tramadol. I've been taking one or two at bedtime most nights, even though the back is a lot better. Honestly it helps me sleep, and for a few hours I feel less flat. I didn't mention it because I figured you'd think I was a pill guy.

Thank you for being straightforward about it. What you are describing makes pharmacological sense and does not make you a pill guy. Tramadol is not only an opioid; it also blocks the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, which is part of why it lifts mood for a few hours. That same property is the problem.

**Why tramadol has to stop before we start an antidepressant:**
- **Serotonin syndrome:** tramadol plus a serotonergic antidepressant can cause agitation, tremor, muscle twitching or clonus, sweating, fever, diarrhea, and a rapid heart rate. Severe cases are a medical emergency.
- **Fluoxetine (Prozac) is a particularly bad pairing:** besides the additive serotonin effect, fluoxetine strongly inhibits the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which normally converts tramadol to its active opioid metabolite. Tramadol then accumulates in its parent form, which raises serotonin toxicity and seizure risk while giving less pain relief. This is a **major** interaction.
- **Seizure threshold:** tramadol lowers it, and so does bupropion (Wellbutrin). That combination is one I would avoid.
- **Using an opioid to manage mood and sleep** carries a risk of escalating use and masks the depression we are trying to treat.

**Plan for the tramadol and your back:** take no more tramadol starting tonight. At roughly 50 to 100 mg nightly for five weeks, significant withdrawal is unlikely, but a few nights of restlessness, aching, or worse sleep can happen; call the care manager if it is more than that. Because tramadol clears within about two days, we will start the antidepressant after **48 hours** without it. For the back, use acetaminophen **1000 mg up to three times daily** (no more than **3 g per day**), heat, and a physical therapy referral that Dr. Nguyen can place. I would limit ibuprofen to occasional use, because regular NSAIDs combined with an SSRI increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Would you be willing to bring the remaining tablets to a pharmacy take-back kiosk?
Yes. There are maybe eight left. I'll drop them at the pharmacy. So which antidepressant?

Here are the main first-line choices, with standard adult doses. Antidepressant doses in adults are not weight-based; at **74 kg** with normal kidney and liver function, standard dosing applies.

| Medication | Starting dose | Usual range | Key points for you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sertraline (Zoloft) | **50 mg** daily | 50 to 200 mg | Well tolerated, few drug interactions, no blood-pressure effect; early nausea and sexual side effects are common |
| Fluoxetine (Prozac) | **20 mg** daily | 20 to 80 mg | Very long half-life, forgiving of missed doses; strong CYP2D6 inhibitor, so more interactions |
| Venlafaxine ER (Effexor XR) | **37.5 to 75 mg** daily | 75 to 225 mg | Serotonin and norepinephrine; dose-related blood-pressure rise; marked discontinuation symptoms |
| Bupropion XL (Wellbutrin XL) | **150 mg** each morning | 150 to 450 mg | Activating, no sexual side effects or weight gain; lowers seizure threshold |
| Mirtazapine | **15 mg** at bedtime | 15 to 45 mg | Helps sleep and appetite; sedation and weight gain |
| Vortioxetine (Trintellix) | **10 mg** daily | 5 to 20 mg | Nausea common; often requires insurance prior authorization |

The largest comparison we have is a 2018 network meta-analysis of 522 trials covering 21 antidepressants (PMID: 29477251). Every antidepressant studied was more effective than placebo. In head-to-head trials, mirtazapine, venlafaxine, and vortioxetine were among the more effective agents and fluoxetine among the less effective, while sertraline, fluoxetine, and vortioxetine were among the better tolerated and venlafaxine had one of the higher dropout rates. The differences between drugs were modest, which is why side-effect profile, interactions, and your preferences drive the choice.

For you, I recommend **sertraline**: strong tolerability, minimal interaction burden, no effect on blood pressure, and a long track record. Mirtazapine is a reasonable alternative given your insomnia and weight loss, but it causes daytime sedation in many people, and you drive to job sites and review technical drawings all day.
What about the sexual side effects? A buddy of mine said Wellbutrin doesn't have those, and he likes it. Why not that one?

Your friend is right that bupropion rarely causes sexual side effects or weight gain, and it is a good medication. There are three reasons I do not favor it as your first choice. First, it tends to be activating, and your early-morning awakening and restlessness at night could get worse at the start. Second, it lowers the seizure threshold in a dose-related way; the risk is about **0.1%** at 300 mg per day in people without risk factors, and it rises with higher doses, recent tramadol use, alcohol binges, or eating disorders. Third, bupropion is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor, which complicates combining it with some other drugs later.

On sexual side effects with sertraline: delayed ejaculation and reduced libido occur in a meaningful minority of men. If that happens and is bothersome, we have options: waiting a few weeks, since some effects fade, adjusting the dose, switching to vortioxetine, or adding bupropion XL **150 mg** each morning, which can offset SSRI-related sexual dysfunction and add antidepressant effect. If we ever combine vortioxetine with bupropion, the vortioxetine dose would be halved because of the CYP2D6 interaction. So the door to bupropion stays open; I would rather not start there.
Okay, that makes sense. I'll try the sertraline. What do I need to know about taking it, and what should I stay away from?

**Sertraline plan:**
- Start **50 mg once daily** with breakfast, beginning the morning after you have gone 48 hours without tramadol. Taking it with food reduces nausea.
- Expect side effects, if any, in the first one to two weeks: nausea, loose stools, headache, jitteriness, or sweating. These usually settle.
- Sleep and appetite often improve first, within two to three weeks; mood and interest usually take four to six weeks, with full effect by eight to twelve.
- Do **not** stop abruptly once you have been on it for a few weeks; that can cause dizziness, irritability, and flu-like discontinuation symptoms.

**Interactions to avoid:**
- **Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs):** this combination is absolutely contraindicated because it can cause fatal serotonin syndrome. That includes phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, and selegiline, and also the antibiotic **linezolid** and the dye **methylene blue** used in some procedures. There must be at least **14 days** between stopping an MAOI and starting sertraline, and 14 days between stopping sertraline and starting an MAOI. Tell any surgeon, emergency physician, or dentist that you take sertraline.
- **Tramadol and other serotonergic drugs:** no tramadol, and check with a pharmacist before using dextromethorphan cough products or St. John's wort.
- **Alcohol:** it worsens depression and sleep; I would keep to no more than one or two drinks on any occasion while we are treating this.

**Warning signs to report promptly:** worsening mood, new agitation or restlessness, or any change from passive thoughts to thoughts of acting. The FDA boxed warning about increased suicidal thoughts applies to people under 25, but we monitor everyone closely in the first weeks.

**Follow-up:** Lucia, our nurse care manager, will call you in **two weeks** to repeat the PHQ-9 and check side effects, and I will see you in **four weeks**. I am also referring you to our therapist for cognitive behavioral therapy; the combination of medication and psychotherapy generally works better than either alone.

Four weeks later, at the follow-up visit: Hi, Dr. Villarreal. So, I stopped the tramadol that night and started the sertraline two days later, like you said. The first three nights off tramadol were rough, legs restless, slept badly, but it passed. The sertraline made me queasy the first week; that's gone. I'm sleeping until about 5:30 now. I've done three sessions with the therapist. The rifle's at Nico's. I filled out the PHQ-9 in the waiting room; I think it was 12. One thing: it's taking a lot longer to finish during sex, which my wife and I have noticed.

Thank you for the detailed update, and for following through on every part of the plan, including the rifle and the tramadol. That was not easy.

**Today's vitals:** BP **122/76 mmHg**, HR **70 bpm**, weight **74.8 kg** (up 0.8 kg from 74.0 kg four weeks ago, which fits your appetite returning).

**PHQ-9:** your score is **12**, down from **19**. That is a **37%** reduction (7 of 19 points). We define a response as at least a 50% reduction and remission as a score below **5**, so you are improving but not yet responding fully. Importantly, your answer to question 9, about thoughts of being better off dead, is now **0**.

You have been on **50 mg** for a little under four weeks with good tolerance. The next step is to increase to **100 mg** once daily with breakfast, starting tomorrow. Clear but partial improvement at four weeks is a good sign that sertraline is the right drug and needs a higher dose.

On delayed ejaculation: this is one of the most common SSRI side effects, and I am glad you mentioned it. It is not dangerous, but it matters to your quality of life and to adherence. At 100 mg it may stay the same or increase modestly. If it remains a problem at our next visit, the two best-supported options are adding bupropion XL 150 mg each morning, which is now reasonable since the tramadol is out of the picture, or switching to vortioxetine. We will decide based on how your mood is doing.
Okay. But what if this doesn't work in the end? My dad went through a few different pills before one stuck. I'm worried I'll be one of those people it never works for.

That concern is reasonable, and the data are more reassuring than your father's experience might suggest. The STAR*D study followed several thousand outpatients with depression through up to four sequential treatment steps (PMID: 17074942). Remission rates were **36.8%** with the first step and **30.6%** with the second, lower in the third and fourth steps, and the overall cumulative remission rate was **67%**. The same study found that people who needed more steps had higher relapse rates during follow-up, which is why we push for full remission rather than settling for partial improvement.

If sertraline at an optimized dose (up to **150 to 200 mg**) is not enough after six to eight weeks, the next options are:
- **Switch** to venlafaxine ER (starting 75 mg, then 150 to 225 mg, with blood-pressure checks), vortioxetine 10 to 20 mg, or mirtazapine 15 to 45 mg at bedtime.
- **Augment** sertraline with bupropion XL 150 to 300 mg or mirtazapine 15 to 30 mg at bedtime.
- In more treatment-resistant cases, specialist options include **lithium** augmentation. If lithium were ever combined with venlafaxine, the two have additive serotonergic effects that raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, so that combination would require slow titration, lithium level monitoring, and close watching for tremor, confusion, or muscle twitching.

For now, you are improving on the first step, which is the best predictor of eventual remission. Continuing CBT is also part of what gets people all the way to remission.
That helps. Two last things. How long am I going to be on this? And my brother's wedding is in three weeks. Can I drink there?

**Duration:** once you reach remission, meaning a PHQ-9 below 5 and feeling like yourself, the standard recommendation for a first episode is to continue the same dose for **6 to 12 months** to reduce the risk of relapse. After that, if you are well, we can taper gradually over several weeks, not stop abruptly. People with recurrent episodes or severe episodes are sometimes advised to continue longer, which we would discuss if it applies to you.

**The wedding:** you can drink modestly. Sertraline does not interact with alcohol the way some medications do, but alcohol is a depressant, it fragments sleep, and heavy drinking is associated with worse depression outcomes. I would suggest no more than **two drinks** over the evening, alternating with water, and not skipping your morning dose the next day. And do not drive after drinking.

**Summary of today's plan:**
- Increase sertraline to **100 mg** daily with breakfast, starting tomorrow.
- Continue CBT weekly; continue acetaminophen and physical therapy for the back as needed; no tramadol.
- Rifle stays with Nico until we agree you are in stable remission.
- Lucia will call in two weeks for a PHQ-9 check; I will see you in **four weeks**.
- Call **988** or go to the emergency department if thoughts of being better off dead return with any intent, or call the clinic for new agitation, tremor, fever, or muscle twitching.

You have done the hard parts well, Mateo. Keep going.

common_mistakes.mistake: Starting an antidepressant without screening for past hypomanic or manic episodes
common_mistakes.explanation: A first depressive episode may be the initial presentation of bipolar disorder. Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression can precipitate mania or rapid cycling. Ask specifically about periods of decreased need for sleep with increased energy, and about family history of bipolar disorder, before prescribing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Relying on the patient's medication list without checking the prescription monitoring program
common_mistakes.explanation: Patients frequently omit controlled substances such as tramadol, which is serotonergic, lowers the seizure threshold, and is not detected on standard opiate immunoassays. Combining tramadol with fluoxetine is a major interaction: additive serotonin toxicity plus CYP2D6 inhibition that increases parent tramadol exposure. A PDMP review before prescribing identifies these exposures.

common_mistakes.mistake: Asking vaguely about mood but not directly about suicidal thoughts and firearm access
common_mistakes.explanation: Asking directly about suicidal ideation does not increase risk. A structured screen such as the C-SSRS distinguishes passive from active ideation, and lethal-means counseling (temporary transfer of firearms to a trusted person) is one of the most effective interventions available in the outpatient setting.

common_mistakes.mistake: Judging an antidepressant ineffective after two weeks or leaving a patient on a subtherapeutic dose indefinitely
common_mistakes.explanation: Mood improvement usually takes four to six weeks, but partial improvement by weeks 2 to 4 predicts eventual response. Measurement-based care with serial PHQ-9 scores should guide dose optimization at about four weeks, and the goal is remission (PHQ-9 below 5), since residual symptoms predict relapse.

common_mistakes.mistake: Overlooking the MAOI washout rules and hidden MAOIs
common_mistakes.explanation: Sertraline combined with an MAOI can cause fatal serotonin syndrome. A 14-day gap is required in both directions for sertraline, and at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before an MAOI because of norfluoxetine's long half-life. Linezolid and methylene blue act as MAOIs and are frequently missed in hospital settings.

differential_diagnosis.differentiating_factors: History of at least one manic or hypomanic episode (decreased need for sleep with high energy, pressured speech, grandiosity, impulsive spending). Clues include early onset, atypical features, psychotic depression, postpartum onset, and a family history of bipolar disorder. Antidepressant monotherapy is avoided.

Fatigue, weight gain rather than loss, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, and delayed relaxation of reflexes; elevated TSH with low free T4. A normal TSH effectively excludes primary hypothyroidism as the cause.

Depressive symptoms that begin during intoxication or withdrawal from alcohol, opioids, sedatives, or stimulants, or after starting drugs such as corticosteroids or isotretinoin, and that remit within weeks of abstinence. Timeline of symptom onset relative to substance use is decisive; in this case depression preceded the tramadol by about five weeks.
Chronic depressed mood on most days for at least 2 years, usually with milder symptoms, rather than a discrete episode of recent onset; a major depressive episode can be superimposed on it.

Emotional or behavioral symptoms that arise within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, are out of proportion to it, and do not meet full criteria for a major depressive episode; neurovegetative features such as early-morning awakening and weight loss favor MDD.

related_diseases.relationship: Highly comorbid with MDD, sharing genetic risk and responding to many of the same agents (SSRIs, SNRIs); comorbid anxiety predicts a slower response and greater side-effect sensitivity at treatment initiation.

Bidirectional relationship with depression; alcohol worsens mood and sleep and increases suicide risk, and substance-induced depression must be distinguished from independent MDD. Heavy use or withdrawal also increases bupropion-associated seizure risk.

related_diseases.disease: Chronic pain (including chronic low back pain)
related_diseases.relationship: Pain and depression amplify each other, and pain management choices interact with antidepressants: tramadol adds serotonin syndrome and seizure risk, and regular NSAID use with SSRIs increases gastrointestinal bleeding risk.

Depression is an independent risk factor for incident coronary disease and worse outcomes after myocardial infarction; SSRIs such as sertraline have established safety data in patients with cardiac disease.
Often presents first with a depressive episode and is misdiagnosed as unipolar MDD; screening for prior hypomania or mania is required before antidepressant monotherapy.

original.executive_summary: **Major depressive disorder (ICD-10 F32.9)** in a 34-year-old biracial civil engineer presenting with ten weeks of anhedonia, early-morning awakening, 4 kg (5%) weight loss, psychomotor slowing, guilt, impaired concentration, and passive death wishes without plan or intent (PHQ-9 **19**). Workup (CBC, CMP with anion gap 11 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, B12, folate, HbA1c, testosterone, urine drug screen) excluded medical mimics, and bipolar screening was negative. A PDMP review uncovered undisclosed nightly **tramadol** use, which was stopped with a 48-hour washout before starting **sertraline 50 mg daily**, given the serotonin syndrome and seizure risks (and the major CYP2D6 interaction with fluoxetine). Safety measures included C-SSRS screening, firearm transfer to a family member, a written safety plan, and 988 counseling; MAOI contraindications and the 14-day washout were reviewed. At four weeks, PHQ-9 fell to **12** (37% reduction, item 9 now 0) with delayed ejaculation, and sertraline was increased to **100 mg**, with bupropion augmentation or a switch to vortioxetine held in reserve. Evidence cited: Cipriani 2018 network meta-analysis (PMID: 29477251), STAR*D cumulative remission of 67% (PMID: 17074942), and the GBD 2020 pandemic-era burden estimate (PMID: 34634250). Plan: CBT, measurement-based titration toward remission (PHQ-9 below 5), then 6 to 12 months of continuation treatment.

facts.answer: Bojím se o mámu, syna, práci i peníze. Přeskakuje to z jednoho na druhé celý den a nedokážu to zastavit.

original.name: GAD
original.description: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive, and uncontrollable worry about multiple life domains (health, finances, work, family) for at least 6 months, accompanied by physical symptoms including restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance. It is highly comorbid with depression, other anxiety disorders, and somatic symptom disorders, significantly impairing function. First-line treatment includes SSRIs/SNRIs and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT); buspirone is an effective anxiolytic alternative to benzodiazepines for long-term use.

drug_interactions.description: Serotonin syndrome risk from combined SNRI and serotonergic opioid.
Combination can cause severe hypertensive episodes; MAOIs must be discontinued 14 days before starting buspirone.
Combined CNS and respiratory depression significantly increases overdose and death risk.
